He reports severe left upper quadrant abdominal pain radiating upward to his left shoulder.
Physical examination reveals localized tenderness, guarding, and left flank bruising.
FAST ultrasound examination of the abdomen confirms free fluid in Morrison pouch and around the spleen.
Contrast-enhanced CT shows a parenchymal tear deeper than 3 cm in the left upper quadrant organ, with active contrast extravasation.
A 48-year-old man visits the ER reporting the sudden generalized abdominal pain.
He notes that the pain started in his upper abdomen after a heavy meal and rapidly spread across his entire stomach.
Physical examination reveals a rigid, board-like abdomen with severe generalized tenderness and rebound guarding.
Auscultation demonstrates completely absent bowel sounds across all four abdominal quadrants.
Upright chest radiography reveals free air under both leaves of the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum).
Emergency exploratory laparotomy confirms a perforated anterior duodenal ulcer requiring primary closure and omental patching.
A 25-year-old woman is brought to the ER after in a suicide attempt.
She reports ingesting a large quantity of over-the-counter medication 12 hours ago and currently experiences mild nausea and right upper quadrant discomfort.
Physical examination reveals a drowsy patient with mild epigastric tenderness and no asterixis.
Laboratory evaluation shows a serum acetaminophen level plotted well above the Rumack-Matthew treatment nomogram line.
Liver function tests reveal rapidly rising serum transaminases (AST and ALT) entering the thousands.
Immediate administration of intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) prevented fulminant hepatic failure.
Paramedics report finding the patient in a poorly ventilated garage with a running gasoline generator.
A 40-year-old man is brought to the ER by paramedics presenting with severe throbbing headache, dizziness, and nausea.
Physical examination reveals cherry-red coloration of the skin and mucous membranes alongside confusion.
Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates normal partial pressure of oxygen with a severely depressed oxygen saturation.
Co-oximetry blood panel confirms an elevated carboxyhemoglobin level of 35%.
Patient is treated successfully with 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask, achieving rapid clinical recovery.
A 30-year-old marathon runner collapses outdoors while running and is rushed to the ER.
Paramedics report finding the patient sweating profusely.
Vital signs demonstrate a core body temperature of 40.8°C, tachycardia, and hypotension.
Neurological examination reveals altered mental status ranging from confusion to obtundation.
Laboratory tests show early evidence of rhabdomyolysis, elevated serum transaminases, and coagulopathy.
Immediate whole-body ice-water immersion cooling restores normal core body temperature and prevents organ failure.
A 19-year-old college student with type 1 diabetes is brought to the ER complaining of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.
Friends report she has experienced excessive thirst, frequent urination, and lethargy over the past 48 hours.
Physical examination reveals dry mucous membranes, delayed capillary refill, and deep, rapid breathing.
Exhaled breath has a distinct, fruity, sweet acetone odor.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates hyperglycemia, a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, and ketonuria.
Treatment with aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, insulin infusion, and electrolyte repletion stabilizes the patient.
A 60-year-old woman visits the ER reporting sudden, severe pain in her right eye.
She notes seeing colored halos around streetlights and experiencing associated nausea and vomiting.
Physical examination reveals a red eye with a mid-dilated pupil that reacts poorly to light.
Slit-lamp examination demonstrates a shallow anterior chamber and corneal epithelial edema.
Tonometry measurement confirms markedly elevated intraocular pressure exceeding 45 mmHg.
Emergency treatment with topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, and pilocarpine lowers pressure prior to laser iridotomy.
A 58-year-old man visits the eye clinic complaining of a sudden onset of flashing lights and dark floaters in his left eye.
He reports that a dark shadow resembling a curtain has progressively swept across his peripheral visual field.
Visual acuity testing demonstrates moderately reduced vision in the affected eye, while the right eye remains normal.
External examination reveals normal pupillary reflexes and no external signs of trauma or redness.
Slit-lamp exam shows clear media with occasional pigmented cells in the anterior vitreous.
Dilated fundoscopic examination confirms a grey, opaque, billowing retina separated from the underlying pigment epithelium.
A 72-year-old woman visits the eye clinic reporting a gradual, painless blurring of her vision over several months.
She notes that straight lines appear wavy and distorted when reading the morning newspaper.
Visual acuity testing reveals difficulty reading fine print, though her peripheral vision remains completely intact.
External eye examination is normal with clear corneas and reactive pupils.
Amsler grid testing confirms central visual distortion (metamorphopsia).
Fundoscopic examination demonstrates numerous yellowish extracellular deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium.
A 28-year-old industrial worker is rushed to the ER after an alkaline cleaning solution splashes into his right eye.
He reports intense burning pain, tearing, and an inability to open his right eyelid.
Physical examination reveals severe eyelid swelling, conjunctival injection, and epithelial corneal defects.
pH paper testing of the conjunctival fornices reveals an alkaline pH remaining above 8.5.
Emergency management begins immediately with continuous normal saline irrigation until neutral pH is restored.
Slit-lamp exam following irrigation shows areas of corneal whitening and ischemia.
A 22-year-old man visits the urgent care clinic complaining of sore throat.
He reports difficulty swallowing his own saliva, resulting in drooling, and a thick, muffled "hot potato" voice.
Physical examination reveals a temperature of 38.9°C and trismus limiting full mouth opening.
Oropharyngeal inspection shows asymmetric swelling of the left soft palate and deviation of the uvula to the right.
Palpation demonstrates tender ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
Needle aspiration yields purulent fluid, confirming the diagnosis and providing immediate symptomatic relief.
A 4-year-old unvaccinated child is brought to the ER with rapid-onset high fever and respiratory distress.
Parents note the child is sitting in a forward-leaning "tripod" position, struggling to breathe and swallow.
Physical examination reveals muffled, quiet voice production and inspiratory stridor without a barking cough.
Attempts to examine the oropharynx are avoided to prevent precipitating complete airway obstruction.
Lateral neck radiography demonstrates a characteristic enlarged, cherry-red epiglottis known as the "thumbprint sign."
Emergency airway management in the operating room secures a stable breathing tube.
A 52-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of recurrent brief episodes of spinning dizziness.
She notes that the vertigo is triggered instantly whenever she rolls over in bed or tilts her head backward.
She reports each episode lasts less than a minute and is occasionally accompanied by mild nausea.
Neurological and cranial nerve examinations are completely normal with no focal deficits or hearing loss.
Dix-Hallpike maneuver elicits delayed-onset torsional nystagmus and vertigo when the affected ear is turned downward.
Symptoms resolve successfully following performance of the particle-repositioning Epley maneuver.
A 55-year-old carpenter visits the orthopedic clinic complaining of persistent pain in his right shoulder.
He notes that the discomfort worsens when he attempts to lift objects overhead or reach behind his back.
He recalls experiencing a sudden sharp pain after catching a falling heavy wooden board at work.
Physical examination reveals decreased active range of motion with a painful arc between 60 and 120 degrees.
Drop-arm test demonstrates the patient's inability to lower the arm slowly from abduction without it dropping suddenly.
Magnetic resonance imaging confirms a full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon.
A 38-year-old recreational tennis player visits the orthopedic clinic reporting a sudden sharp snap in his left ankle.
He states it felt as though someone kicked him in the back of his leg while sprinting across the court.
Physical examination reveals localized swelling and a palpable defect or gap along the tendon proximal to the calcaneus.
Active plantarflexion of the ankle is significantly weakened and limited.
Squeezing the calf muscle while the patient lies prone fails to produce plantarflexion, yielding a positive Simmonds-Thompson test.
MRI confirms a complete disruption of the Achilles tendon fibers.
A 45-year-old accountant who recently started woodworking visits the clinic reporting elbow pain.
She notes that the pain worsens when gripping objects, turning doorknobs, or lifting coffee mugs.
Physical examination reveals localized tenderness directly over the lateral epicondyle of the humerus.
Resisted wrist extension with the elbow fully extended reproduces the sharp local pain (Cozen test).
Range of motion of the elbow joint is fully preserved without locking or joint effusion.
Plain radiographs of the elbow are normal, confirming tendinopathy of the extensor carpi radialis brevis.
A 42-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of persistent fatigue and weight gain.
She notes dry skin, hair thinning, and mild constipation over the past several months.
Physical examination reveals a firm, non-tender, symmetrically enlarged goiter.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates an elevated serum TSH level and low free T4 concentration.
Thyroid ultrasound shows a diffuse heterogeneous echotexture with hypervascularity.
Serological testing confirms high titers of circulating anti-thyroperoxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies.
A 35-year-old man visits the clinic presenting recurrent kidney stones.
Laboratory evaluation reveals persistent hypercalcemia, elevated serum parathyroid hormone, and high fasting gastrin levels.
Brain MRI demonstrates a pituitary macroadenoma associated with elevated prolactin levels.
Family history is significant for multiple endocrine tumors in a first-degree relative.
Genetic testing confirms a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene encoding menin.
Clinical diagnosis establishes primary hyperparathyroidism, a gastrinoma, and a prolactinoma.
A 38-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of progressive abdominal swelling and right upper quadrant pain.
Her medical history includes a newly diagnosed hypercoagulable state due to factor V Leiden mutation.
Physical examination reveals tense ascites, hepatomegaly, and prominent superficial abdominal wall veins.
Liver function tests show mildly elevated transaminases and hyperbilirubinemia.
Doppler ultrasound demonstrates thrombosis of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava.
Liver biopsy confirms centrilobular congestion and sinusoidal dilation.
A 40-year-old woman visits the cardiology clinic reporting progressive shortness of breath with daily exertion.
She notes experiencing occasional lightheadedness and chest discomfort when walking up hills.
Physical examination reveals a loud pulmonic second heart sound and a prominent parasternal lift.
Electrocardiogram demonstrates right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Transthoracic echocardiography estimates a significantly elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure.
Right heart catheterization confirms pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
A 30-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers and genital sores.
He notes developing a tender erythematous nodular skin rash on his lower extremities.
Physical examination reveals multiple painful oral ulcers and scarring genital lesions alongside anterior uveitis.
Pathergy test demonstrates a positive sterile pustule formation 48 hours after skin prick testing.
Laboratory tests show an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate and normal autoantibody panels.
A pathergy test is positive, with a sterile pustule forming 48 hours after a needle prick, alongside the recurrent oral and genital ulcers.
A 3-year-old toddler is brought to the pediatrician by parents reporting low-grade fever and poor oral intake.
Parents note the child is irritable and refuses to eat.
Physical examination reveals vesicular lesions on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and soft palate.
Examination also shows small, tender red papules and vesicles on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet.
Vital signs show mild fever resolving within several days with supportive care.
Clinical presentation confirms common enteroviral infection caused by Coxsackievirus A16.
A 42-year-old man visits the ENT clinic complaining of persistent nasal blockage and loss of smell.
He notes constant post-nasal discharge and dull facial pressure across his cheekbones.
His medical history includes severe allergic rhinitis and aspirin sensitivity.
Anterior rhinoscopy reveals pale, translucent masses filling both nasal cavities.
Flexible nasal endoscopy confirms smooth, non-tender polyps originating from the middle meatus.
Sinus CT scan demonstrates opacification of the ethmoid and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
A 52-year-old woman is rushed to the ER with acute respiratory distress and severe dysphagia.
She reports a history of generalized weakness and experiencing progressive worsening of her double vision and drooping eyelids over the past week despite taking her standard medication.
Physical examination reveals shallow, labored breathing, weak cough, and marked bulbar weakness with inability to manage oral secretions.
Negative inspiratory force (NIF) and vital capacity measurements demonstrate impending respiratory failure.
Ice pack test previously showed temporary improvement of ptosis, confirming neuromuscular junction blockade.
Emergency endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation are initiated alongside plasmapheresis.
A 45-year-old man visits the ER complaining of progressive weakness in his feet over five days.
He reports experiencing mild tingling and numbness in his toes and fingertips, accompanied by severe lower back aching.
He notes recovering from a mild diarrheal illness caused by Campylobacter jejuni three weeks prior.
Physical examination reveals absent deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities and ascending motor weakness.
Lumbar puncture demonstrates classic albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated CSF protein and normal cell count.
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies confirm acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
A 38-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of several episodes of severe headaches.
He notes these episodes last 20 to 30 minutes and are accompanied by intense anxiety and pallor.
Vital signs during a clinic visit reveal a sudden blood pressure spike of 210/120 mmHg alongside tachycardia.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates markedly elevated 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines.
Computed tomography of the abdomen identifies a well-circumscribed, highly vascular mass arising from the adrenal medulla.
Patient is treated successfully with alpha-blockade preparation followed by surgical adrenalectomy.
A 74-year-old man is brought to the neurology clinic by his family due to progressive gait difficulties.
Family members report he walks with a slow, magnetic, broad-based gait and has experienced frequent unexplained falls.
They also note he has developed urinary urgency, frequent incontinence and cognitive slowing over the past several months.
Mini-Mental State Examination reveals mild subcortical dementia with psychomotor slowing and executive dysfunction.
Brain MRI demonstrates disproportionate ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal widening.
Large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) results in temporary gait improvement, predicting successful ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement.
A 58-year-old man visits the neurology clinic complaining of progressive muscle weakness in his right hand.
He notes noticing involuntary rippling movements under the skin of his upper arms and frequent muscle cramps.
Physical examination reveals combined upper and lower motor neuron signs, including muscle wasting, fasciculations, and hyperreflexia.
Examination demonstrates both weakness of limb muscles and early bulbar signs with slight dysarthria.
Sensory examination is entirely normal, with no deficits in touch, pain, or vibration.
Electromyography confirms widespread denervation and reinnervation across multiple spinal segments.
A 45-year-old man who suffered a penetrating stab wound to the chest is rushed to the emergency room in severe distress.
Vital signs reveal profound hypotension, and markedly distended neck veins.
Physical examination demonstrates pulsus paradoxus with a drop in systolic blood pressure exceeding 15 mmHg during inspiration.
Electrocardiogram shows low-voltage QRS complexes and electrical alternans.
Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (FAST) confirms a large pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium and ventricle.
Emergency pericardiocentesis immediately relieves the hemodynamic collapse prior to definitive surgical repair.
A 48-year-old female presents with progressive cognitive decline, confusion, and clumsiness in her left arm over 6 weeks.
She reports a history of SLE treated with long-term immunosuppressive therapy

Physical examination reveals left-sided motor weakness, sensory ataxia, visual field deficits (left homonymous hemianopsia), and prominent aphasia without signs of elevated intracranial pressure or fever.

Brain MRI (T2/FLAIR) demonstrates asymmetric, non-enhancing white matter hyperintensities involving the subcortical white matter of the parieto-occipital lobes that do not exhibit mass effect or perilesional edema.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis shows normal cell count and protein, but qualitative PCR testing for JC virus DNA is highly positive.
Stereotactic brain biopsy confirms demyelination, bizarre astrocytes, and enlarged oligodendrocytes with amphophilic intranuclear viral inclusions.
A 68-year-old retired industrial worker visits the pulmonology clinic complaining of a persistent cough and progressive shortness of breath over two years.
He reports that his dyspnea has worsened gradually from occurring only during heavy exertion to limiting basic daily activities.
Physical examination reveals fine, high-pitched "Velcro-like" inspiratory crackles at the lung bases and digital clubbing.
Pulmonary function testing demonstrates a restrictive pattern with decreased total lung capacity and reduced diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide.
Arterial blood gas analysis shows resting hypoxemia that worsens significantly with physical exertion.
High-resolution computed tomography of the chest reveals peripheral subpleural reticular opacities and honeycombing with traction bronchiectasis.
A 34-year-old African American woman visits the clinic complaining of persistent dry cough and fatigue.
She notes experiencing mild shortness of breath and vague anterior chest discomfort when walking outdoors.
Physical examination reveals bilateral tender erythematous subcutaneous nodules on the anterior shins (erythema nodosum).
Laboratory evaluation reveals mild hypercalcemia and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels.
Chest radiography demonstrates prominent bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and right paratracheal lymph node enlargement.
Transbronchial biopsy confirms non-caseating granulomas without evidence of fungal or mycobacterial infection.
A 42-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of progressive fatigue and pruritus.
He reports having an intermittent right upper quadrant discomfort, and also a 10-year history of ulcerative colitis
Laboratory evaluation reveals an obstructive liver enzyme pattern with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase.
Serum bilirubin levels are mildly elevated, and antimitochondrial antibodies return strictly negative.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) demonstrates multifocal strictures and segmental dilations throughout the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts, producing a characteristic "beaded" appearance.
Liver biopsy reveals concentric periductal "onion-skin" fibrosis surrounding the bile ducts.
A 19-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his family due to a progressive behavioral change.
Physical examination reveals a resting and intention tremor, rigidity.
Laboratory evaluation shows low serum ceruloplasmin levels and elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion.
Liver function tests reveal moderately elevated transaminases alongside signs of chronic cirrhosis.
Slit-lamp examination confirms the presence of Kayser-Fleischer rings.
Genetic testing identifies mutations in the ATP7B gene, confirming impaired biliary copper excretion.
A 38-year-old man visits the ER complaining of a progressive, dull headache and low-grade fever over two weeks.
He notes that the headache has gradually worsened and is accompanied by intermittent confusion and lethargy.
he mentions a history of advanced HIV infection and a CD4 count of 65 cells/microliter
Physical examination reveals mild neck stiffness, though classic meningeal signs are subtle.
Lumbar puncture demonstrates an elevated opening pressure, normal to low glucose, elevated protein, and clear cerebrospinal fluid.
CSF India ink stain reveals encapsulated yeast cells, and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) assay returns strongly positive.
A 52-year-old man visits the neurology clinic reporting progressive cognitive decline, personality changes.
Examination demonstrates impaired position and vibration sense in the lower extremities alongside a wide-based, slapping gait.
Mental status evaluation reveals memory deficits, emotional lability, and poor calculation skills.
Physical examination reveals irregular pupils that constrict poorly to light but retain constriction during accommodation (Argyll Robertson pupils).
Serum VDRL and FTA-ABS tests return strongly reactive.
Lumbar puncture shows a lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis, raised CSF protein and a reactive CSF-VDRL.
A 48-year-old man visits the clinic complaining recurrent bloody nasal discharge.
He reports developing a persistent cough, hemoptysis, and pleuritic chest pain over the past month, alongside dark, tea-colored urine.
Laboratory workup reveals elevated serum creatinine and active urinary sediment with red blood cell casts.
Chest radiography demonstrates bilateral nodular pulmonary infiltrates with areas of cavitation.
Serological evaluation shows high titers of anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies directed against proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA).
Renal biopsy confirms pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis.
A 45-year-old woman visits the rheumatology clinic complaining of pain in her fingers when exposed to cold temperatures.
She notes that her fingers turn white, then blue, and finally red.
Physical examination reveals sclerodactyly, loss of digital skin folds, telangiectasias on the face, and microstomia.
She reports experiencing frequent severe heartburn and dysphagia due to esophageal dysmotility.
Serological testing demonstrates positive anti-centromere antibodies.
Capillaroscopy reveals dilated capillary loops and avascular areas in the nailfold beds.
A 21-year-old male presents with gross hematuria, moderate generalized edema.
He reports a history of a viral upper respiratory infection.
Laboratory evaluation reveals nephrotic-range proteinuria (4.5 g/24h), microscopic hematuria with red blood cell casts, and elevated serum creatinine (2.1 mg/dL).
Complement studies show profoundly depressed serum C3 levels with normal C4 levels, alongside the presence of C3 nephritic factor (C3NeF) autoantibodies.
Renal biopsy light microscopy reveals membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) patterns with mesangial cellular proliferation.

Transmission electron microscopy of the glomeruli demonstrates continuous, highly characteristic ribbon-like extremely electron-dense deposits located within the basement membrane of the glomerular capillaries.
A 6-year-old child is brought to the pediatric emergency room with decreased urine output.
Parents report the child attended a petting zoo and consumed undercooked meat a week prior.
Physical examination reveals pallor, petechiae, jaundice, and mild peripheral edema without hepatosplenomegaly.
Complete blood count demonstrates microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on the peripheral blood smear, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury.
Stool cultures and Shiga-toxin assays confirm infection with enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7.
Management focuses on supportive care, fluid management, and avoiding antibiotics to prevent toxin release.
A 50-year-old man visits the clinic for a routine physical examination and is found to have splenomegaly.
Complete blood count reveals a marked leukocytosis with a total white blood cell count exceeding 150,000/microliter.
Peripheral blood smear demonstrates a full spectrum of myeloid differentiation, including myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands, and segmented neutrophils, alongside basophilia.
Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is profoundly low.
Bone marrow aspirate reveals hypercellularity with prominent granulocytic proliferation.
Cytogenetic analysis confirms the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome ( translocation producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene).
A 65-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of a pain in his lower back that worsens with movement.
He reports experiencing frequent respiratory infections, and noting excessive thirst.
Laboratory evaluation reveals normocytic anemia, elevated serum total protein with a normal albumin level, and renal insufficiency.
Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) demonstrates a prominent monoclonal spike (M-protein), and urinalysis confirms Bence-Jones proteins.
Skeletal survey radiographs reveal multiple lytic "punched-out" bone lesions across the skull, spine, and pelvis.
Bone marrow biopsy confirms greater than 10% clonal plasma cell infiltration.
A 48-year-old man with a history of severe alcohol use disorder is hospitalized for acute abdominal pain.
On the third hospital day, he suddenly becomes profoundly confused, disoriented, and agitated.
Physical examination reveals tremors, profuse diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and visual hallucinations (seeing crawling insects).
Vital signs show a temperature of 38.8°C and severe autonomic instability.
Neurological evaluation confirms hyperactive delirium secondary to abrupt alcohol withdrawal.
Immediate administration of high-dose intravenous benzodiazepines controls agitation and prevents seizures.
A 35-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department with altered mental status.
Family members report he has developed extreme muscle stiffness, confusion, and high fever over the past 24 hours.
Physical examination reveals generalized "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity, diaphoresis, labile blood pressure, and tachycardia.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a markedly elevated serum creatine kinase level and acute leukocytosis.
A member of the family confirms recent initiation of a high-potency first-generation antipsychotic medication for his schizophrenia.
Immediate discontinuation of the offending agent and administration of dantrolene or bromocriptine supports recovery.
A 32-year-old woman in active labor experiences sudden cardiovascular collapse and severe respiratory distress.
Vital signs reveal profound hypotension, cyanosis, and sudden cardiac arrest within minutes.
Physical examination and continuous monitoring demonstrate non-reassuring fetal heart tones progressing rapidly to fetal bradycardia.
Laboratory evaluation reveals acute consumptive coagulopathy with severe bleeding from intravenous sites and profuse postpartum hemorrhage.
Pathophysiology involves maternal immune-mediated activation triggered by entry of fetal antigens into the maternal circulation.
Emergency perimortem Cesarean delivery and aggressive hemodynamic resuscitation are initiated immediately.

disease: Gestational Trophoblastic Disease (Molar Pregnancy – hydatidiform mole)
clues: A 24-year-old woman visits the gynecology clinic reporting first-trimester vaginal bleeding.
She notes that her uterine size appears significantly larger than expected for her 10 weeks of gestational age.
Pelvic examination reveals passage of grape-like vesicular tissue fragments through the external os.
Quantitative serum beta-hCG levels are markedly elevated well above normal expected ranges for gestational age.
Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a classic "snowstorm" appearance within the uterine cavity without an embryonic pole.
Suction curettage confirmed the diagnosis, prompting baseline post-evacuation surveillance.
A premature neonate born at 28 weeks gestation develops bloody stools on the tenth day of life.
Physical examination reveals a tense, shiny, discolored abdominal wall with visible dilated loops of bowel.
Vital signs demonstrate lethargy, apnea, and metabolic acidosis requiring mechanical ventilator support.
Complete blood count shows thrombocytopenia and bandemia indicative of severe sepsis.
Abdominal radiography demonstrates pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall) and portal venous gas.
Emergency exploratory laparotomy confirms extensive bowel necrosis requiring surgical resection.
A newborn infant is evaluated for having macrocephaly and hydrocephalus.
Maternal history reveals consumption of undercooked meat and gardening without gloves during the first trimester of pregnancy.
Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rash ("blueberry muffin" spots), microcephaly, and chorioretinitis.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows elevated protein and mononuclear pleocytosis.
Serological testing confirms the presence of specific anti-toxoplasma IgM and IgG antibodies in both mother and infant.
Cranial imaging confirms diffuse intracranial calcifications distributed throughout the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia.
A 56-year-old man visits the emergency department reporting the sudden onset of severe lower chest and upper abdominal pain.
Physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema palpable in the suprasternal notch and diminished breath sounds at the left lung base.
Symptoms occurred after multiple episodes of forceful vomiting following a heavy meal.
Erect chest radiography reveals a left-sided pleural effusion, widened mediastinum, and air in the soft tissues of the neck.
Water-soluble contrast swallow esophagography confirms contrast extravasation from the lower left posterolateral wall of the esophagus.
Emergency surgical exploration and primary repair with mediastinal drainage are performed.
A 7-year-old child is evaluated for chronic foul-smelling greasy stools (steatorrhea), abdominal distension, failure to thrive over the past several years.
Physical examination reveals peripheral neuropathy with absent deep tendon reflexes, loss of proprioception and vibratory sense, and atypical pigmentary retinopathy.
Complete blood count shows normocytic anemia, and peripheral blood smear reveals prominent acanthocytes (thorny, spiky red blood cells) accounting for over 50% of circulating erythrocytes.
Serum lipid profile demonstrates profoundly undetectable levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and fasting chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL.
Duodenal mucosal biopsy demonstrates villous architecture containing enterocytes packed with lipid droplets in their cytoplasm due to an inability to export fats.
Molecular testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the MTTP gene (encoding microsomal triglyceride transfer protein).
A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after intentionally ingesting a large quantity of an unknown drug in an attempt to suicide.
Physical examination reveals a lethargic, obtunded patient with dry skin, mydriasis, resting tachycardia, and delayed bowel sounds.

12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus tachycardia, prolonged PR interval, widened QRS complex exceeding 100 milliseconds, and a right axis shift of the terminal 40-ms vector of the QRS (prominent R wave in aVR).
Patient experiences a sudden generalized tonic-clonic seizure followed by refractory hypotension.
Arterial blood gas reveals an underlying metabolic acidosis.
Emergency management includes intravenous sodium bicarbonate boluses to narrow the QRS complex and stabilize cardiac membranes.
A 45-year-old woman is brought to the ER presenting with persistent nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, and rapid deep breathing.
Family members report she ingested excessive amounts of oil of wintergreen over the past 24 hours.
Physical examination reveals hyperventilation, diaphoresis, and mild confusion.
Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates a primary high anion gap metabolic acidosis concurrent with a primary respiratory alkalosis.
Serum salicylate level confirms severe systemic toxicity well above the therapeutic threshold.
Treatment involves alkalinization of the urine using intravenous sodium bicarbonate drips and consideration of hemodialysis for refractory cases.
A 68-year-old man visits the emergency department reporting sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in his left eye.
He notes that the visual loss occurred instantaneously while he was reading the morning newspaper.
Visual acuity testing confirms bare light perception only in the affected eye, with a normal right eye examination.
He mentions he have a long term history of severe atherosclerosis and hypertension
Relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) is prominently present on the left side.

Dilated fundoscopic examination demonstrates a pale, ischemic retinal background with a striking "cherry-red spot" at the fovea and carotid duplex ultrasound reveals high-grade stenosis of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery.
A 74-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of a new-onset headache, accompanied by profound fatigue.
She notes experiencing sharp pain in her jaw muscles when chewing food and persistent aching in her shoulders.
Physical examination reveals a tender, nodular, and pulseless right temporal artery with overlying skin erythema.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) exceeding 90 mm/hr and high C-reactive protein.
Patient is at immediate risk for permanent ischemic optic neuropathy and sudden blindness.
Temporal artery biopsy confirms granulomatous inflammation centered on the internal elastic lamina, establishing the diagnosis.
A 42-year-old man visits the emergency department reporting severe neck swelling, pain, and difficulty swallowing.
Physical examination reveals a woody, indurated swelling of the floor of the mouth, bilateral submandibular fullness, and upward displacement of the tongue.
Vital signs demonstrate high fever, tachycardia, and a muffled "hot potato" voice.
He reports a history of neglected dental caries
Patient exhibits early signs of respiratory compromise with stridor and pooling of oral secretions.
Computed tomography of the neck confirms deep space cellulitis and soft tissue gas tracking through the sublingual and submandibular spaces.
A 22-year-old man is brought to the trauma center following a crush injury to his right calf from heavy machinery.
He reports severe, deep, bursting pain in his calf that is completely unresponsive to high-dose intravenous narcotic pain medications.
Physical examination reveals a tense, swollen calf with extreme pain elicited upon passive extension of the toes.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are fully palpable, and distal sensation remains intact, demonstrating that pulses are preserved despite ischemia.
Needle manometry confirms intracompartmental pressure within 30 mmHg of the diastolic blood pressure.
Immediate emergency double-incision four-compartment fasciotomy is performed to prevent irreversible muscle infarction.
A 38-year-old woman is rushed to the ER with extreme agitation, high fever, and vomiting.
Vital signs reveal a body temperature of 40.5°C, a heart rate of 165 bpm, and a wide pulse pressure with mild systolic hypertension.
A member of the family mentions she had a history of Graves disease and stopped taking her antithyroid medications
Physical examination demonstrates a diffusely enlarged goiter, tremor, warm moist skin, and mild delirium.
Laboratory workup confirms markedly elevated free T3 and free T4 levels with suppressed TSH.
The Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale score is well above 45, and urgent treatment with propranolol, propylthiouracil and hydrocortisone begins.
A 29-year-old man hospitalized following a severe traumatic brain injury develops massive polyuria and extreme thirst.
Nursing records show a urine output exceeding 300 ml per hour of very pale, dilute urine over the past four hours.
Laboratory evaluation reveals hypernatremia, a high serum osmolality, and a concurrently low urine osmolality.
Water deprivation test demonstrates a failure to concentrate urine, followed by a significant increase in urine osmolality after the administration of exogenous desmopressin (DDAVP).
Brain MRI confirms loss of the normal posterior pituitary bright spot.
After desmopressin is given, urine osmolality rises by more than 50% and urine output falls sharply.
A 58-year-old man visits the ER complaining of diffuse abdominal pain and worsening confusion.
Physical examination reveals shifting dullness, diffuse abdominal tenderness across all quadrants, and absent rebound guarding.
He had a history of alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites.
Diagnostic paracentesis is performed; peritoneal fluid analysis reveals a polymorphonuclear (PMN) leukocyte count exceeding 250 cells/mm3.
Ascitic fluid total protein is low, and Gram stain is frequently negative despite active infection.
Intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy with third-generation cephalosporins is initiated successfully.
A 54-year-old man undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia develops persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain, and hemoptysis.
Physical examination reveals tachypnea and diminished breath sounds over the right upper lung field.
Laboratory evaluation shows profound neutropenia, and chest radiography demonstrates a pulmonary nodule.
Serum galactomannan assay returns strongly positive.
High-resolution CT scan shows a nodule with a surrounding halo of ground-glass attenuation (halo sign), followed by an air-crescent sign as the neutrophil count recovers.
Sputum and tissue cultures confirm angioinvasive infection with Aspergillus fumigatus.
A 56-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of severe, persistent bone pain in both lower legs, progressive fatigue, and insidiously worsening balance problems and urinary frequency.
Physical examination reveals bilateral, symmetric pitting edema around the knees and ankles, exophthalmos (proptosis) of both eyes, and xanthelasma-like yellowish plaques on the eyelids.
Plain radiographs of the long bones reveal characteristic symmetric, bilateral cortical osteosclerosis of the diaphysis and metaphysis of the distal femurs and proximal/distal tibiae.
Skeletal scintigraphy (technetium-99m bone scan) demonstrates intense, pathognomonic symmetric tracer uptake in the diaphyseal and metaphyseal regions of the long bones.
Biopsy of a bone lesion confirms infiltration by lipid-laden foamy histiocytes surrounded by fibrosis, which stain positive for CD68 and CD168, but negative for CD1a and S100.
Molecular genetic testing identifies the somatic BRAF V600E mutation, allowing targeted therapy with vemurafenib to achieve clinical response.
A 55-year-old farmer visits the emergency department reporting painful muscle spasms.
Physical examination reveals trismus with a fixed, sardonic grin (risus sardonicus) and generalized muscle rigidity.
He notes that he cut his hand on a rusty piece of farm equipment two weeks ago and did not seek medical attention or receive a booster vaccination.
Minimal tactile or auditory stimuli trigger severe, painful generalized muscle spasms and opisthotonos.
Autonomic instability manifests as labile blood pressure, tachycardia, and profuse sweating.
Treatment begins with human immune globulin against the bacterial toxin, wound debridement, metronidazole and ventilatory support.
A 40-year-old traveler is brought to the emergency department with painful spasms of the throat muscles.
He mentions a history of traveling in a rural area abroad two months prior and failing to receive post-exposure prophylaxis.
Physical examination reveals hypersalivation, autonomic instability, and violent pharyngeal spasms triggered by the sight of water or any attempt to drink.
Neurological status rapidly deteriorates from fluctuating agitation to coma and brain death.
History of animal exposure combined with clinical signs establishes the diagnosis, supported by fluorescent antibody staining of skin biopsy or saliva PCR.
The disease is almost always fatal once clinical symptoms manifest.
Four members of a family are brought to the emergency department having blurred vision, and progressive descending muscle weakness.
Physical examination reveals bilateral fixed dilated pupils, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and dry mucous membranes.
Sensation remains entirely intact, and mental status is completely clear throughout the examination.
They report eating home-canned green beans at dinner the previous evening.
Electromyography demonstrates an incremental response to high-frequency repetitive nerve stimulation, confirming neuromuscular blockade.
Administration of equine botulinum antitoxin and supportive respiratory care halt disease progression.
A 10-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic complaining of polyarthritis affecting the knees, ankles, and wrists.
Physical examination reveals a new apical holosystolic murmur, subcutaneous nodules, and a faint erythematous non-pruritic rash with central clearing (erythema marginatum).
Parents report the child had a sore throat three weeks ago that resolved without antibiotic treatment.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, high C-reactive protein, and positive anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers.
Electrocardiogram shows a prolonged PR interval indicating first-degree atrioventricular block.
The antistreptolysin O titer is markedly raised, and the findings together meet the modified Jones criteria.
A 2-year-old toddler is brought to the pediatric emergency department with high-grade fever for the past six days.
Physical Examination shows polymorphous erythematous rash across the trunk and edema with peeling skin on the palms and soles.
Examination also reveals bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, a bright red "strawberry" tongue, and dry, cracked lips.
Patient exhibits tender cervical lymphadenopathy measuring greater than 1.5 cm in diameter.
Laboratory workup demonstrates leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, and elevated inflammatory markers.
Treatment with high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and aspirin prevents coronary artery aneurysm formation.
A 48-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of severe fatigue, unintended weight loss.
He reports developing numbness and weakness in his right foot (foot drop) and new-onset high blood pressure, and painful tender lumps on his lower legs.
Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated inflammatory markers, normocytic anemia, and negative ANCA serology.
Serological testing confirms chronic hepatitis B virus infection in a subset of cases.
Computed tomography angiography of the mesenteric or renal vasculature demonstrates multiple microaneurysms and areas of stenosis.
Tissue biopsy confirms necrotizing vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries sparing the pulmonary circulation.
A 28-year-old woman visits the vascular clinic complaining of fatigue, dizziness, and painful cramping in her arms when lifting objects.
Physical examination reveals absent or markedly diminished pulses in both upper extremities, earning the condition its historic moniker.
Vital signs demonstrate a significant blood pressure discrepancy exceeding 15 mmHg between the right and left arms.
Auscultation reveals continuous bruits audible over the subclavian arteries and the abdominal aorta.
Laboratory workup shows elevated acute-phase reactants, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein.
Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrates severe stenosis, occlusion, and aneurysm formation of the aorta and its primary branches.
A 36-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of pain in her fingers when exposed to cold.
She notes swelling of her hands, making her fingers appear sausage-like (dactylitis), alongside muscle weakness and heartburn.
Physical examination reveals sclerodactyly, Raynaud phenomenon, and mild symmetric polyarthritis.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a high titer of speckled antinuclear antibodies.
Specific serology confirms the presence of antibodies directed against ribonucleoprotein (anti-U1-RNP) in the absence of other extractable nuclear antigens.
Clinical features overlap manifestations seen in systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, and polymyositis.
A 56-year-old man hospitalized with severe acute pancreatitis develops sudden, progressive shortness of breath and tachypnea.
Vital signs reveal hypoxemia refractory to supplemental oxygen delivered via standard nasal cannula.
Physical examination demonstrates bilateral diffuse crackles without signs of fluid overload or elevated left atrial pressure.
Chest radiography reveals diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates sparing neither lung field.
Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrates a severely depressed PaO2/FiO2 ratio falling below 200 mmHg.
Management requires endotracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation with low tidal volumes, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).
A 60-year-old heavy smoker visits the emergency department complaining of high fever, dry cough, and progressive shortness of breath.
Physical examination reveals a temperature of 39.5°C, relative bradycardia (Faget sign), and coarse rales over the right lung base.
He reports returning from a hotel convention in a coastal city five days prior.
Laboratory workup demonstrates hyponatremia, elevated liver transaminases, and microscopic hematuria.
Chest radiography reveals patchy unilateral alveolar infiltrates progressing to consolidation.
Urine antigen test confirms infection with Legionella pneumophila.
A 45-year-old pet store owner visits the clinic complaining of high fever, severe headache, dry cough, and generalized muscle aches.
Physical examination reveals a temperature of 39.0°C, relative bradycardia, and mild hepatosplenomegaly.
He reports spending the past week cleaning cages and handling newly imported exotic parrots.
Chest radiography demonstrates prominent interstitial infiltrates out of proportion to physical examination findings.
Laboratory tests show normal white blood cell count despite high fever, alongside elevated liver enzymes.
Serology confirms acute infection with Chlamydia psittaci, treated successfully with doxycycline.
A 32-year-old triathlete visits the emergency department complaining of high fever, severe headache, and pain in his calves.
Physical examination reveals conjunctival suffusion without purulent discharge, calf tenderness, and mild jaundice.
He reports participating in a freshwater swimming race through muddy rural floodwaters two weeks ago.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated total bilirubin, disproportionately high serum creatinine relative to blood urea nitrogen, and thrombocytopenia.
Serological testing or microscopic agglutination test confirms infection with Leptospira interrogans.
Mild cases respond well to oral doxycycline, while severe Weil disease requires intensive supportive care and intravenous penicillin.
A 38-year-old veterinarian visits the clinic complaining of chronic on and off fevers, and profound fatigue.
He reports frequent joint aches, and unintentional weight loss over the past six weeks.
He notes a history of assisting with difficult livestock births on local dairy farms without wearing protective gloves.
Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and tender vertebral percussion over the lumbar spine.
Blood cultures incubated on specialized media isolate small gram-negative coccobacilli, confirmed as Brucella species.
Combination antibiotic therapy with doxycycline and aminoglycosides or rifampin achieves cure and prevents relapse.
A 42-year-old farmer visits the clinic complaining of severe headache, and dry cough.
Physical examination reveals a temperature of 39.2°C, relative bradycardia, and mild hepatomegaly.
Chest radiography demonstrates segmental opacity consistent with atypical pneumonia.
He reports assisting during lambing season on his farm three weeks prior.
Laboratory evaluation shows normal leukocyte count and elevated liver function tests.
Serology confirms acute infection with Coxiella burnetii, treated successfully with a two-week course of doxycycline.
A 30-year-old landscape worker visits the clinic complaining of a painful ulcer on his right hand.
Vital signs demonstrate high-grade fever, chills, and fatigue.
Physical examination reveals an erythematous, punched-out ulcer with a black base on the right index finger alongside large matted lymphadenopathy.
He reports cutting brush and removing rabbit nests from overgrown fields a week prior.
History of animal contact combined with ulceroglandular presentation guides diagnosis, confirmed by serology or fluorescent antibody staining.
Treatment with intramuscular streptomycin or oral doxycycline achieves complete resolution.
A 48-year-old textile worker is rushed to the emergency department complaining of fever and dry cough.
Physical examination reveals diaphoresis, cyanosis, and tachypnea without signs of upper airway obstruction.
He reports that his symptoms rapidly progressed over 24 hours to include severe shortness of breath and substernal chest pain.
Chest radiography demonstrates a markedly widened mediastinum and bilateral pleural effusions without primary pulmonary infiltrates.
Gram stain of blood cultures isolates large, encapsulated, gram-positive rod-shaped bacteria in chains (Bacillus anthracis).
Multidrug intravenous antibiotic therapy and antitoxin administration are initiated immediately in an intensive care setting.
A 35-year-old hiker living in the southwestern United States visits the emergency department with sudden high fever and severe pain in his right groin.
Physical examination reveals an extremely tender, enlarged, fluctuant lymph node in the right inguinal region.
Complete blood count demonstrates severe leukocytosis and elevated inflammatory markers.
He reports camping in an area with rodent burrows and finding dead wild rodents prior to symptom onset.
Gram stain of needle aspirate from the bubo reveals safety-pin shaped gram-negative bacilli (Yersinia pestis).
Immediate administration of streptomycin or gentamicin resolves the infection.
A 50-year-old diabetic traveler returning from Southeast Asia visits the emergency department complaining of fever, productive cough, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain.
Physical examination reveals localized tenderness over the liver and coarse breath sounds.
Chest radiography demonstrates bilateral nodular infiltrates with cavitation mimicking tuberculosis.
Blood and sputum cultures isolate bipolar-staining gram-negative bacilli (Burkholderia pseudomallei).
Abdominal ultrasound identifies multiple small microabscesses within the liver and spleen.
Prolonged intravenous treatment followed by months of oral eradication therapy is required to prevent high mortality.
A 45-year-old immigrant from South America visits the cardiology clinic complaining of progressive shortness of breath and palpitations.
Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular heartbeat, elevated jugular venous pressure, and peripheral edema.
Electrocardiogram demonstrates right bundle branch block and left anterior fascicular block.
Echocardiography shows marked cardiomegaly with severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction and apical aneurysm.
History notes living in a rural mud-brick home infested with triatomine kissing bugs during childhood.
Serology confirms chronic infection with Trypanosoma cruzi.
A 28-year-old traveler returning from East Africa visits the clinic complaining of prolonged irregular fevers, profound weight loss.
Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly and generalized hyperpigmentation of the skin.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates pancytopenia, hypoalbuminemia, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.
Bone marrow aspirate examined under microscopy reveals intracellular amastigotes (Leishmania Donovan bodies) within macrophages.
Serological testing confirms high titers of anti-leishmanial antibodies.
Intravenous liposomal amphotericin B therapy achieves complete parasitological cure.
A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family due to progressive confusion and lethargy over two days.
Family members note he has been sleeping during the day, staying awake at night, and expressing bizarre behavioral changes.
Physical examination reveals a slow, coarse flapping tremor of outstretched hands (asterixis) and a musty, sweet breath odor (fetor hepaticus) and a cirrhotic liver.
Mental status evaluation demonstrates disorientation to time and space alongside poor attention span.
Serum laboratory workup reveals elevated venous ammonia levels, precipitating factors including mild hypokalemia and constipation.
Treatment with oral lactulose and rifaximin lowers ammonia production and restores normal mental status.
A 58-year-old man is hospitalized due to rapidly progressive oliguria.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates a rising serum creatinine level exceeding 2.5 mg/dl over a week without prior intrinsic kidney disease.
Urinalysis shows normal sediment with no proteinuria and a very low fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa under 1%).
He had a history of end-stage cirrhosis and refractory ascites
Intravenous fluid challenge with albumin fails to improve renal function or increase urine output.
Pathophysiology involves severe renal vasoconstriction secondary to systemic arterial vasodilation mediated by portal hypertension.
A 65-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and intense generalized pruritus.
Physical examination reveals icteric sclera and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder.
He reports experiencing a dull right upper quadrant ache and unintentional weight loss of 10 kg over the past two months.
Laboratory evaluation reveals an obstructive liver enzyme profile with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and direct bilirubin.
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) demonstrates a stricture at the confluence of the right and left hepatic ducts (Klatskin tumor).
Histological biopsy confirms malignant adenocarcinoma originating from the biliary epithelium.
A 29-year-old woman is rushed to the emergency department with acute confusion, and rapid-onset right upper quadrant pain.
Physical examination reveals asterixis, fetor hepaticus, and a shrinking liver span on percussion.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates severe coagulopathy with an international normalized ratio (INR) exceeding 1.5 and markedly elevated serum transaminases.
Mental status rapidly deteriorates into hepatic encephalopathy and cerebral edema.
History reveals accidental massive acetaminophen ingestion combined with heavy alcohol use.
Patient is listed urgently for emergency orthotopic liver transplantation alongside supportive intensive care management.
A 22-year-old college basketball player visits the cardiology clinic for evaluation after his brother experienced sudden cardiac arrest.
He reports occasional episodes of exertional chest pain and lightheadedness when running down the court.
Physical examination reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border that intensifies during the Valsalva maneuver.
Electrocardiogram demonstrates deep Q waves in the inferior and lateral leads alongside prominent left ventricular hypertrophy voltages.
Transthoracic echocardiography confirms asymmetric thickening of the interventricular septum and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve.
Genetic screening identifies an autosomal dominant mutation in genes encoding cardiac sarcomere proteins.
A 64-year-old man visits the cardiology clinic complaining of progressive shortness of breath, and fatigue.
Physical examination reveals elevated jugular venous pressure with a prominent  and  descent, bilateral pedal edema, and an S3 gallop.
Electrocardiogram demonstrates low-voltage QRS complexes despite echocardiographic evidence of ventricular wall thickening.
Transthoracic echocardiography shows normal or reduced ventricular volumes, biatrial enlargement, and impaired diastolic filling with preserved ejection fraction.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirms characteristic subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement.
Endomyocardial biopsy establishes the underlying diagnosis of cardiac amyloidosis.
A 28-year-old man visits the emergency department complaining of sharp chest pain and progressive shortness of breath.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated cardiac biomarkers (troponin I and CK-MB) and an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
Physical examination reveals a soft S3 gallop, tachycardia, and a friction rub.
Electrocardiogram shows diffuse non-specific ST-segment and T-wave abnormalities.
He reported a history of a viral flu-like illness.
Endomyocardial biopsy confirms lymphocytic infiltration and myocyte necrosis consistent with viral inflammatory cardiomyopathy.
A 32-year-old woman visits the endocrine clinic presenting with recurrent episodes of sweating, and palpitations.
Physical examination reveals a firm, painless thyroid nodule in the left lobe.
Family history is significant for thyroid cancer and adrenal tumors in multiple first-degree relatives.
Laboratory evaluation confirms elevated plasma and urinary metanephrines, alongside elevated serum calcitonin levels.
Genetic testing confirms a germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene.
Clinical diagnosis establishes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and primary hyperparathyroidism.
A 20-year-old man visits the clinic presenting with long slender limbs, and skeletal deformities.
Physical examination reveals multiple small mucosal neuromas appearing as bumpy nodules on his lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa.
Family history reveals aggressive thyroid malignancy.
Laboratory workup reveals elevated calcitonin levels and positive screening for catecholamine excess.
Genetic testing confirms a specific missense mutation in the RET proto-oncogene.
Clinical diagnosis establishes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and mucosal neuromas without hyperparathyroidism.
A 16-year-old adolescent boy visits the nephrology clinic for evaluation of persistent hematuria.
Family history reveals that his maternal grandfather and uncle both reached end-stage renal disease at a young age.
Ophthalmologic examination reveals anterior lenticonus and dot-and-fleck retinopathy.
Audiometric testing confirms bilateral high-tone sensorineural hearing loss.
Renal biopsy electron microscopy demonstrates characteristic alternating thickening and thinning of the glomerular basement membranes with splitting of the lamina densa ("basket-weave" appearance).
Genetic testing confirms X-linked mutations in the COL4A5 gene encoding type IV collagen.
A 32-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of painful burning sensations in his hands and feet that worsen with exercise and heat.
Physical examination reveals a cluster of dark red, non-blanching vascular skin lesions distributed across his bathing suit area and umbilicus.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates early renal impairment with mild proteinuria and progressive kidney failure.
Ophthalmologic slit-lamp examination shows characteristic corneal whorls (cornea verticillata).
Assay of peripheral leukocytes demonstrates deficient activity of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A.
Genetic testing confirms an X-linked deficiency leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular endothelial cells.
A 52-year-old man visits the neurology clinic presenting with progressively worsening insomnia, and cognitive slowing over several months.
Physical examination reveals subtle myoclonus, ataxia, resting tachycardia, excessive sweating, and a low-grade fever.
Sleep studies (polysomnography) demonstrate a total loss of slow-wave and REM sleep patterns alongside disrupted circadian rhythms.
Family history is notable for a similar progressive neurodegenerative condition affecting multiple maternal relatives.
Positron emission tomography (PET) scans show profound bilateral thalamic hypometabolism.
Genetic sequencing confirms a missense mutation in the PRNP gene (D178N substitution coupled with methionine at codon 129), establishing the prion disorder.
A 45-year-old woman visits the neurology clinic complaining of progressive, painful muscle stiffness and rigidity in her lower back and legs.
She notes that minor sensory stimuli, such as unexpected loud noises or light touch, trigger severe, violent muscle spasms and falls.
Physical examination reveals hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine and board-like rigidity of the paraspinal and abdominal muscles.
Electromyography demonstrates continuous motor unit activity in agonist and antagonist muscles at rest.
Serological testing reveals exceptionally high titers of antibodies directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD).
Treatment with high-dose diazepam, baclofen, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) provides symptomatic relief.
A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department reporting acute onset of double vision, unsteadiness, and progressive lethargy following a mild upper respiratory infection.
Physical examination reveals ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, hyperreflexia, and a positive Babinski sign.
Lumbar puncture demonstrates classic albuminocytologic dissociation with elevated cerebrospinal fluid protein and normal cell count.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain shows high-intensity signal abnormalities in the brainstem tegmentum.
Serological evaluation confirms high titers of anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies, linking the condition to Guillain-Barré spectrum disorders.
Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy leads to gradual and complete neurological recovery.
A 12-year-old child is brought to the pediatric neurology clinic by his parents due to progressive behavioral changes, declining school performance, and myoclonic jerks.
Parents note he had a history of primary measles infection when he was 18 months old before receiving vaccination.
Electrocardiogram-triggered electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrates periodic, stereotyped high-voltage slow-wave complexes (Radermecker complexes) recurring synchronously every few seconds.
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis reveals normal cell count, elevated protein, and extremely high titers of anti-measles virus antibodies.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging reveals progressive white matter demyelination and cortical atrophy.
The condition follows a relentlessly progressive and ultimately fatal neurodegenerative course.

disease: MELAS Syndrome (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like Episodes)
clues: A 24-year-old woman visits the neurology clinic reporting recurrent stroke-like episodes, focal seizures, and severe migraine headaches.
She notes a lifelong history of short stature, exercise intolerance, and progressive sensorineural hearing loss.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates resting lactic acidosis with elevated serum lactate-to-pyruvate ratios.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging reveals stroke-like lesions that do not respect major vascular territories, typically involving the parietal and temporal lobes.
Skeletal muscle biopsy demonstrates classic "ragged-red fibers" on modified Gomori trichrome staining, confirming mitochondrial dysfunction.
Genetic testing identifies the characteristic m.3243A>G mutation in the mitochondrial MT-TL1 gene.
A 38-year-old man is brought to the psychiatric clinic by his family due to progressive personality changes, depression.
Family history reveals his father suffered from a similar neurodegenerative disorder starting in middle age and died prematurely.
Physical examination reveals choreiform movements affecting the face, trunk, and extremities alongside impaired saccadic eye movements.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrates severe atrophy of the caudate nuclei and putamen.
Genetic testing confirms an abnormal expansion of cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) trinucleotide repeats exceeding 39 repeats in the HTT gene on chromosome 4p16.3.
The disorder follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with complete penetrance and genetic anticipation.

disease: Dunbars Syndrome (Median Arcuate Ligament Syndrome / MALS)
clues: A 24-year-old lean woman presents with severe postprandial epigastric pain occurring 20 minutes after eating, also reports weight loss over 6 months.
Physical examination reveals a thin abdomen with a soft systolic bruit audible in the epigastrium during full expiration that disappears on deep inspiration.
Diagnostic workup including upper endoscopy, gastric emptying studies, abdominal ultrasound, and colonoscopy are completely unrevealing.
Mesenteric Doppler ultrasound demonstrates elevated peak systolic velocities (>200 cm/s) in the celiac artery during expiration that normalize during deep inspiration.
Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT angiography demonstrates a characteristic hooked appearance of the proximal celiac artery with focal narrowing during expiration.
Laparoscopic surgical division of the median arcuate ligament and ganglionectomy results in immediate relief of postprandial pain and weight recovery.
A 10-year-old child is evaluated for developmental delay, infantile spasms, and hypopigmented macules shaped like ash leaves under Wood lamp examination.
Physical examination reveals firm, reddish-brown angiofibromas distributed symmetrically across the nasal bridge and cheeks (adenoma sebaceum).
Examination also shows shagreen patches on the lower back and subungual fibromas around the toenails.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging reveals subependymal nodules and cortical tubers along the cerebral ventricles.
Echocardiography identifies a benign cardiac rhabdomyoma.
Genetic testing confirms a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene that normally restrains the mTOR signaling pathway.
A 25-year-old man visits the clinic for evaluation of multiple flat, hyperpigmented skin spots and soft subcutaneous nodules.
Physical examination reveals more than six café-au-lait spots measuring greater than 1.5 cm in diameter alongside axillary and inguinal freckling.
Slit-lamp ophthalmologic examination identifies multiple pigmented iris hamartomas.
Examination demonstrates numerous cutaneous neurofibromas and early skeletal dysplasia involving the sphenoid wing.
Family history is positive for similar cutaneous findings in his mother.
Genetic testing identifies an inactivating mutation in a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17q11.2 encoding neurofibromin.
A newborn infant is evaluated for a prominent dark red birthmark covering the forehead and upper eyelid in the distribution of the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve.
Parents report the infant experienced focal motor seizures affecting the contralateral side of the body within the first few months of life.
Ophthalmologic evaluation reveals elevated intraocular pressure and congenital glaucoma in the ipsilateral eye.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrates leptomeningeal angiomatosis with classic "tram-track" cortical calcifications.
Neurological examination shows progressive contralateral hemiparesis and cognitive impairment.
Pathophysiology involves a somatic mosaic mutation in the GNAQ gene affecting vascular development.
A 22-year-old tall, slender college student visits the clinic complaining of sudden onset sharp chest pain and shortness of breath.
Ophthalmologic evaluation confirms bilateral superior lens dislocation (ectopia lentis).
Physical examination reveals a marfanoid body habitus with long, spider-like fingers (arachnodactyly), hypermobile joints, and pectus excavatum.
Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrates marked aortic root dilation and mitral valve prolapse.
Family history reveals a parent who experienced sudden aortic dissection at a young age.
Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15q21 encoding fibrillin-1.
A 28-year-old woman visits the vascular surgery clinic presenting with spontaneous rupture of the sigmoid colon.
Joint hypermobility is relatively mild and largely limited to the digits.
Family history is notable for sudden premature death in a sibling due to arterial rupture.
Physical examination reveals translucent skin with visible underlying veins, easy bruisability, and characteristic facial features including prominent eyes and a thin nose.
Patient is at extreme risk for life-threatening vascular, uterine, and bowel ruptures with minimal trauma.
Genetic testing confirms a heterozygous mutation in the COL3A1 gene encoding type III procollagen.
A newborn infant delivered preterm is evaluated for severe skeletal deformities, and respiratory distress.
Physical examination reveals an extremely soft cranium, shortened limbs with micromelia, and distinctive blue sclerae.
Family history is generally negative, representing a de novo autosomal dominant mutation.
Radiographic skeletal survey demonstrates multiple fractures of the ribs, long bones, and spine with classic " beaded" ribs and crumpled long bones.
Infants born with this severe form typically succumb to respiratory failure shortly after birth.
Genetic testing identifies structural mutations in either the COL1A1 or COL1A2 genes encoding type I collagen.
An infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for profound hypotonia, poor feeding.
By early childhood, the patient develops an insatiable appetite leading to severe obesity, behavioral outbursts, and obsessive-compulsive traits.
Physical examination reveals almond-shaped eyes, down-turned corners of the mouth, small hands and feet (acromicria), and hypopigmentation.
Endocrine evaluation confirms hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and growth hormone deficiency.
Cytogenetic methylation analysis and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) demonstrate a microdeletion on the paternal chromosome 15q11-q13.
Clinical management requires strict dietary environmental control and growth hormone replacement therapy.
A 3-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of developmental delay, absence of speech.
Physical examination shows microcephaly, a prominent jaw, and widely spaced teeth.
Examination also reveals characteristic jerky, puppet-like ataxic movements, a wide-based gait, and hyperactive deep tendon reflexes.
the child has a happy demeanor with frequent inappropriate laughter.
Electroencephalography demonstrates abnormal, highly characteristic runs of high-amplitude delta activity.
Genetic testing confirms a maternal microdeletion on chromosome 15q11-q13 or mutation of the UBE3A gene.
A 5-year-old child is evaluated for global developmental delay, cardiovascular abnormalities.
Cardiovascular examination reveals a loud systolic ejection murmur radiating to the neck.
Physical examination reveals distinctive "elfin" facial features, including a broad forehead, full cheeks, a short nose with a depressed nasal bridge, and a wide mouth with full lips.
Echocardiography confirms supravalvular aortic stenosis and peripheral pulmonary stenosis.
Psychological evaluation demonstrates an outgoing, overly friendly personality, strong verbal skills alongside profound visuospatial construction deficits.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) confirms a microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23 encompassing the elastin gene.
A newborn infant is evaluated for cyanotic congenital heart disease, and recurrent infections.
Physical examination reveals dysmorphic facial features, including low-set ears, micrognathia, and a cleft palate.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates profound hypocalcemia secondary to congenital hypoparathyroidism and leading to neonatal tetany,.
Immunological workup shows severe T-cell lymphopenia due to congenital thymic aplasia.
Echocardiography confirms truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot.
Genetic testing identifies a microdeletion on the long arm of chromosome 22 at band q11.2.
An 8-year-old child is brought to the hematology clinic for evaluation of progressive fatigue, pallor, and easy bruising.
Complete blood count demonstrates progressive pancytopenia with macrocytic anemia.
Physical examination reveals abnormal skin pigmentation (café-au-lait spots), short stature, and congenital skeletal malformations such as thumb and radial ray anomalies.
Cytogenetic analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes exposed to diepoxybutane (DEB) shows a markedly elevated rate of chromosomal breakage.
Bone marrow biopsy confirms profound hypocellularity and aplastic anemia.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive or X-linked mutations in DNA cross-link repair pathway genes.
A 6-year-old child is brought to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of severe sunburns, and skin lesions following minimal sun exposure.
Physical examination reveals marked solar elastosis, hyperpigmented macules resembling freckles on sun-exposed areas, and early cutaneous carcinomas.
Ophthalmologic examination demonstrates chronic photophobia, keratitis, and corneal opacification.
A subset of patients develops progressive neurological degeneration and intellectual disability (De Sanctis-Cacchione syndrome).
Pathophysiology involves an inherited defect in nucleotide excision repair genes, preventing the repair of UV-induced thymine dimers.
Strict lifelong sun avoidance and protective gear form the cornerstone of management.
An infant is evaluated for generalized skin fragility and blistering occurring immediately upon minor mechanical friction or trauma.
Physical examination reveals tense fluid-filled blisters distributed primarily over the hands, feet, and areas subjected to mechanical stress.
Biopsy with immunofluorescence mapping demonstrates intraepidermal cleavage occurring within the basal keratinocyte layer.
Unlike more severe forms of epidermolysis bullosa, lesions typically heal without significant scarring or permanent contractures.
Family history indicates an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in genes encoding keratins 5 or 14 (KRT5 or KRT14).

disease: Epidermolysis Bullosa Dystrophica (Recessive Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa)
clues: A newborn infant is evaluated for severe generalized blistering, fragile skin, and localized absence of skin at birth (congenital aplasia cutis).
Physical examination reveals widespread fragile blisters that heal with severe atrophic scarring, mitten deformity fusion of the fingers (pseudosyndactyly), and nail dystrophy.
Oral examination demonstrates mucosal strictures, microstomia, and severe dental caries.
Transmission electron microscopy and immunofluorescence mapping confirm blister cleavage below the lamina densa within the papillary dermis.
Genetic testing identifies autosomal recessive mutations in the COL7A1 gene encoding type VII collagen, which forms anchoring fibrils.
Patients face a markedly elevated lifetime risk of developing aggressive squamous cell carcinomas on scarred areas.
An infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for widespread erythroderma, severe scaling, and failure to thrive.
Physical examination reveals fragile, short, sparse scalp hair and eyebrows that break easily.
Microscopic examination of hair shafts under light microscopy reveals characteristic "bamboo hair" (trichorrhexis invaginata) showing ball-and-socket telescoping deformities.
Laboratory workup reveals profound hypernatremic dehydration due to massive transcutaneous water loss, alongside high serum IgE levels and peripheral eosinophilia.
Pathophysiology involves unchecked proteolytic activity in the stratum corneum due to loss-of-function mutations in the SPINK5 gene encoding LEKTI.
Management requires intensive supportive care, barrier repair, and careful avoidance of topical calcineurin inhibitors due to systemic absorption risks.
A female newborn infant is evaluated for a distinctive vesicular skin rash distributed in linear whorls along the lines of Blaschko.
Parents note the rash evolves over months through distinct stages: vesicular, verrucous (warty), swirling hyperpigmentation ("marble cake" pattern), and finally hypopigmented atrophic scars.
Physical examination reveals patchy alopecia, nail dystrophies, and dental anomalies such as peg-shaped or missing teeth.
Ophthalmologic evaluation reveals proliferative retinopathy, strabismus, and risk of permanent retinal detachment.
Neurological screening uncovers microcephaly, developmental delay, and recurrent focal seizures.
Genetic testing confirms an X-linked dominant mutation in the IKBKG (NEMO) gene, which is embryonic lethal in males.
A 2-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of a persistent reticulated rash on the cheeks that has spread to the extremities.
Physical examination reveals poikiloderma featuring a combination of telangiectasias, mottled hyperpigmentation, and hypopigmentation over the face and extensor surfaces.
Examination also shows sparse scalp hair, absent eyelashes or eyebrows, juvenile cataracts, and congenital short stature.
Skeletal survey demonstrates radial ray defects and hypoplastic thumbs or patellae.
Affected individuals develop premature aging features and carry a significantly elevated lifetime risk of osteosarcoma and skin cancers.
Genetic testing identifies autosomal recessive mutations in the RECQL4 gene encoding a DNA helicase.
An infant is evaluated for painful blistering of the hands and feet occurring after minimal sun exposure or mechanical trauma.
Physical examination reveals progressive generalized poikiloderma, cutaneous atrophy, and pronounced photosensitivity that improves slightly with age.
Examination demonstrates diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma and painful pseudosyndactyly of the fingers.
Mucosal involvement includes urethral, anal, and esophageal strictures accompanied by severe gingivitis and periodontitis.
Transmission electron microscopy shows cleavage occurring at multiple levels within the basement membrane zone.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive loss-of-function mutations in the FERMT1 gene encoding kindlin-1.
An adolescent visits the dermatology clinic complaining of extremely thick, discolored fingernails and toenails that curve upward like miniature ram horns.
Physical examination reveals prominent hypertrophic nail dystrophy affecting all twenty digits, accompanied by extremely painful, debilitating focal palmoplantar keratoderma.
