Examination also shows oral leukokeratosis on the tongue and buccal mucosa, along with multiple epidermal inclusion cysts and follicular keratosis.
Patient reports severe difficulty walking due to recurrent subungual blistering and plantar callosities.
Family history indicates an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high penetrance.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in keratin genes, most commonly KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT6C, or KRT16.
A young child is brought to the dermatology clinic for evaluation of severe, mutilating palmoplantar keratoderma and periorificial keratotic plaques.
Physical examination reveals symmetric, sharply demarcated, yellowish-brown thickening of the palms and soles with severe flexion contractures of the fingers (pseudoainhum).
Examination also shows severe follicular hyperkeratosis surrounding the mouth, eyes, and perineal region, accompanied by universal alopecia and nail dystrophy.
Patient experiences intense chronic pruritus, pain, and foul-smelling bacterial superinfection over hyperkeratotic fissures.
Histopathological evaluation reveals marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and parakeratosis.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the TRPV3 gene encoding a transient receptor potential cation channel.
Physical examination reveals firm, greasy, yellowish-brown papules distributed over seborrheic areas, including the forehead, scalp, central chest, and back.
A 20-year-old man visits the dermatology clinic complaining of persistent, foul-smelling, rough papules on his chest and back that worsen in warm weather.
Examination demonstrates characteristic nail abnormalities featuring longitudinal white and red alternating stripes and distinctive V-shaped distal notches.
Oral examination reveals pebble-like mucosal cobblestoning of the hard palate.
Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy reveals pathognomonic dyskeratotic cells known as corps ronds and grains, accompanied by suprabasal acantholysis.
Genetic testing confirms an autosomal dominant mutation in the ATP2A2 gene encoding the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase pump (SERCA2).
A 30-year-old woman visits the dermatology clinic complaining of recurrent, painful, weeping erosions and macerated plaques in her armpits and groin folds.
She notes that the skin lesions flare up recurrently with friction, heat, and sweating, accompanied by a foul malodor.
Physical examination reveals flaccid vesicles and erosions that rupture easily, forming crusted fissured plaques in intertriginous zones.
Histopathological examination reveals extensive intraepidermal acantholysis spanning almost the entire thickness of the epidermis, resembling a dilapidated brick wall ("fadograph" appearance).
Family history indicates an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with variable penetrance.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the ATP2C1 gene encoding a Golgi apparatus calcium pump.
A 10-year-old child is brought to the clinic complaining of severe, immediate burning pain, itching, and redness on sun-exposed areas of skin within minutes of outdoor exposure.
Parents note that despite the intense pain, there is minimal visible blistering or edema, distinguishing it from other porphyrias.
Physical examination reveals mild lichenification, scarring, and waxy thickening over the nose and knuckles after chronic sun exposure.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates normal urinary porphyrins alongside markedly elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin and plasma porphyrins.
Hepatobiliary evaluation is critical due to the risk of protoporphyrin-induced cholestatic liver failure and gallstones.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the FECH gene encoding ferrochelatase, or gain-of-function mutations in ALAS2.
An infant is evaluated for severe photosensitivity, blistering skin lesions, and reddish-brown discoloration of urine and teeth.
Physical examination reveals mutilating scarring, sclerodermatous thickening, and loss of fingers, ears, and nose due to severe chronic phototoxic destruction.
Examination under Wood lamp illumination shows a brilliant red fluorescence of the teeth (erythrodontia) and urine.
Laboratory workup reveals severe hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and massive urinary excretion of uroporphyrin I and coproporphyrin I.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the UROS gene encoding uroporphyrinogen III synthase.
A 9-year-old boy presents to the pediatric clinic with progressive vision loss, hearing impairment, and unsteadiness while walking over the past 6 months.
Physical examination reveals bilateral optic disc pallor, sensory ataxia, impaired tandem gait, and absent ankle reflexes.
Laboratory testing shows elevated fasting blood glucose, raised HbA1c, and a low urine specific gravity that fails to respond to desmopressin administration.
Brain MRI demonstrates mild cerebellar atrophy along with subtle brainstem signal intensity changes.
Audiometry confirms bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, while fundoscopy shows severe optic atrophy without retinal pigmentation.
Targeted genetic sequencing reveals a pathogenic variant in the WFS1 gene or associated mitochondrial genome loci, confirming the diagnosis.
A 5-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic exhibiting features of premature aging (progeria), microcephaly, and growth failure.
Physical examination reveals cachectic dwarfism, a bird-like facial appearance with a pinched nose and sunken eyes, and severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss.
Ophthalmologic evaluation reveals pigmentary retinopathy ("salt-and-pepper" appearance), optic atrophy, and cataracts.
Neurological examination shows progressive intellectual disability, white matter demyelination, basal ganglia calcifications, and ataxia.
Unlike typical DNA repair disorders, patients exhibit extreme photosensitivity without an increased risk of skin cancers.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the CSA (ERCC8) or CSB (ERCC6) genes involved in transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair.
A child is evaluated for brittle, fragile hair, scaling skin (ichthyosis), intellectual disability, and short stature.
Polarized light microscopy of scalp hair shafts reveals striking alternating light and dark bands ("tiger-tail" banding pattern).
Chemical analysis of the hair confirms an abnormally low sulfur and cysteine amino acid content.
Patients experience photosensitivity and recurrent infections, reflecting overlapping cellular defects.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in transcription factor IIH (TFIIH) subunit genes such as ERCC2 (XPD) or GTF2H5.
A 6-year-old child is brought to the neurology clinic for evaluation of progressive unsteadiness, poor balance, and involuntary movements when walking.
Physical examination reveals progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, and prominent dilated blood vessels on the bulbar conjunctivae (telangiectasias).
Immunological workup demonstrates recurrent sinopulmonary infections associated with IgA, IgG, and IgE deficiencies.
Laboratory evaluation reveals elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein levels in virtually all affected patients.
Radiotherapy or radiomimetic chemical exposure causes extreme cellular sensitivity and chromosomal instability.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the ATM gene on chromosome 11q22-23 encoding a key DNA damage checkpoint kinase.
A young child is evaluated for microcephaly, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, and distinctive bird-like facial features.
Physical examination reveals sloping forehead, prominent midface, large ears, and mild growth retardation.
Immunological evaluation reveals cellular and humoral immunodeficiency with profound hypogammaglobulinemia and T-cell defects.
Laboratory workup demonstrates extreme cellular hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation with radioresistant DNA synthesis.
Patients carry a dramatically elevated risk of developing lymphoid malignancies and lymphomas at an early age.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the NBS1 gene encoding nibrin.
A 38-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of premature graying of hair, thinning skin, and a hoarse, high-pitched voice.
Physical examination reveals a bird-like facies, generalized taut sclerodermatous skin changes, bilateral cataracts, and muscle wasting in the extremities.
Metabolic evaluation uncovers premature onset of type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, and severe premature coronary artery disease.
Patients exhibit high frequency of soft tissue sarcomas and unusual neoplasms.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the WRN gene encoding a RecQ-type DNA helicase/exonuclease.
A 4-year-old child is brought to the pediatric clinic presenting with striking features of accelerated aging, growth failure, and sclerodermatous skin changes.
Physical examination reveals a disproportionately large head, alopecia, micrognathia, prominent scalp veins, a pinched nose, and joint contractures (pear-shaped thorax).
Cardiovascular evaluation reveals severe premature generalized atherosclerosis leading to myocardial infarctions and strokes in early childhood.
Cognitive development remains completely normal, contrasting sharply with the severe physical aging phenotype.
Family history is negative, representing a de novo sporadic autosomal dominant point mutation.
Genetic testing confirms a recurrent point mutation in the LMNA gene producing an abnormal farnesylated lamin A protein variant called progerin.
A young boy is evaluated for short stature, delayed bone maturation, and characteristic facial and genital anomalies.
Physical examination reveals facial features including ocular hypertelorism, down-slanted palpebral fissures, a broad nasal bridge, and a widow's peak hairline.
Examination also shows brachydactyly, cutaneous syndactyly between fingers, and a characteristic shawl scrotum surrounding the penis.
Radiographic evaluation reveals mild cervical spine anomalies and delayed skeletal maturation.
Family history indicates an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the FGD1 gene encoding a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for Cdc42.
A 16-year-old adolescent girl visits the endocrinology clinic complaining of obesity, rounded face, and short stature.
Physical examination reveals shortening of the fourth and fifth metacarpal and metatarsal bones, resulting in dimpled knuckles when making a fist (Albright sign).
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia with elevated parathyroid hormone levels, reflecting target-organ resistance to PTH.
Patient also exhibits resistance to other peptide hormones, including TSH, gonadotropins, and glucagon.
Pathophysiology involves heterozygous inactivating mutations inherited maternally in the GNAS gene encoding the Gs-alpha stimulatory protein subunit.
Biochemical resistance to PTH distinguishes this condition from true primary hypoparathyroidism.
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric endocrinology clinic presenting with signs of early pubertal development and recurrent bone fractures.
Physical examination reveals large, irregular hyperpigmented skin macules with jagged borders resembling the coast of Maine ("café-au-lait spots").
Endocrinological workup confirms gonadotropin-independent precocious puberty alongside hyperthyroidism and acromegaly.
Radiographic skeletal survey demonstrates polyostotic fibrous dysplasia with thinning of the cortex and cystic lesions.
Pathophysiology arises from a somatic activating post-zygotic mosaic mutation in the GNAS gene.
The mosaic nature of the mutation means clinical manifestations vary widely depending on tissue distribution.
An infant is evaluated for failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, and recurrent episodes of dehydration.
Laboratory evaluation reveals severe hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with normal or low blood pressure despite high plasma renin and aldosterone levels.
Urinalysis demonstrates marked urinary wasting of sodium, chloride, potassium, and calcium (hypercalciuria leading to nephrocalcinosis).
Pathophysiology involves defective salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, mimicking chronic loop diuretic ingestion.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms loss-of-function mutations in genes such as SLC12A1 (NKCC2) or KCNJ1 (ROMK).
A 20-year-old woman visits the clinic complaining of chronic fatigue, muscle cramps, and carpopedal spasms.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis accompanied by marked hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria.
Unlike Bartter syndrome, blood pressure is normal to low and urinary calcium excretion is characteristically reduced.
Pathophysiology involves defective sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, mimicking chronic thiazide diuretic use.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms inactivating mutations in the SLC12A3 gene encoding the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter (NCCT).
A 19-year-old man visits the hypertension clinic for evaluation of severe, treatment-resistant high blood pressure discovered during routine screening.
Laboratory evaluation reveals hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with profoundly suppressed plasma renin activity and low aldosterone levels.
Pathophysiology involves constitutive overactivation of renal epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the collecting ducts, leading to unchecked sodium reabsorption.
Administration of standard mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone) is ineffective, whereas amiloride or triamterene successfully lowers blood pressure.
Family history indicates an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with high penetrance.
Genetic testing confirms gain-of-function mutations in the SCNN1A, SCNN1B, or SCNN1G genes encoding ENaC subunits.
A young male patient is evaluated for low molecular weight proteinuria, hypercalciuria, and recurrent kidney stones (nephrocalcinosis).
Laboratory workup reveals normal serum calcium and phosphate levels, accompanied by progressive renal failure and rickets in some patients.
Urinalysis demonstrates Fanconi-like proximal tubular dysfunction with aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and glycosuria.
Family history reveals X-linked inheritance affecting male maternal relatives.
Ophthalmologic and audiometric evaluations remain entirely normal, distinguishing it from other tubular nephropathies.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the CLCN5 gene encoding a renal chloride-proton exchanger, or OCRL1.
A 25-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of mild, intermittent jaundice triggered by stress, infection, or oral contraceptive use.
Laboratory evaluation reveals conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia with normal serum transaminases and alkaline phosphatase levels.
Total urinary coproporphyrin excretion is normal, but the proportion of coproporphyrin isomer I exceeds 80%.
Gross inspection during laparoscopic surgery or gross liver biopsy reveals a striking characteristic heavily pigmented, jet-black liver.
Pathophysiology involves impaired hepatocyte excretion of bilirubin glucuronides into the bile canaliculi.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the ABCC2 gene encoding MRP2 (multidrug resistance-associated protein 2).
A 20-year-old woman visits the clinic for evaluation of mild, chronic, asymptomatic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
Laboratory evaluation reveals direct hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver transaminases, normal alkaline phosphatase, and normal gallbladder visualization on oral cholecystography.
Unlike Dubin-Johnson syndrome, liver biopsy reveals normal histology without any dark pigment accumulation, and urinary coproporphyrin isomer I is not elevated.
Total urinary coproporphyrin excretion is markedly elevated with a high ratio of isomer III to isomer I.
Pathophysiology involves defective hepatic storage and uptake of organic anions due to dual mutations.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in both the SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 genes encoding hepatic organic anion transporting polypeptides.
A newborn infant develops severe, persistent jaundice within the first 24 hours of life, with total serum bilirubin exceeding 20 mg/dl.
Laboratory evaluation reveals profound unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver enzymes and normal conjugated bilirubin fractions.
Bile analysis demonstrates a total absence of bilirubin glucuronides, reflecting complete lack of enzyme activity.
Infant is at extreme risk for developing irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy (kernicterus) without immediate intervention.
Phototherapy lowers bilirubin levels temporarily, but liver transplantation remains the only definitive cure.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the UGT1A1 gene encoding bilirubin uridine diphosphate-glucuronosyltransferase.
A 32-year-old man visits the hematology clinic complaining of dark urine upon first awakening in the morning, accompanied by severe abdominal pain.
Complete blood count demonstrates cytopenias affecting multiple cell lineages, often overlapping with aplastic anemia.
Laboratory workup reveals hemolytic anemia with elevated lactate dehydrogenase, low haptoglobin, and reticulocytosis, alongside unexplained venous thrombosis (Budd-Chiari syndrome).
Flow cytometry analysis of peripheral blood cells confirms absent surface expression of GPI-anchored proteins, including CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (MIRL).
Pathophysiology involves somatic mutations in the PIGA hematopoietic stem cell gene, rendering red blood cells vulnerable to complement-mediated lysis.
Monoclonal antibody therapy targeting terminal complement (eculizumab) successfully prevents intravascular hemolysis.
A 45-year-old man visits the clinic complaining of chronic fatigue, and joint pain.
Patient develops secondary endocrine and hepatic complications, including diabetes mellitus, cardiomyopathy, and micronodular cirrhosis.
Laboratory evaluation reveals markedly elevated serum ferritin levels and transferrin saturation exceeding 50%.
Liver biopsy demonstrates heavy parenchymal iron deposition predominantly in hepatocytes.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms homozygous C282Y or compound heterozygous C282Y/H63D mutations in the HFE gene on chromosome 6.
A neonate or young child is evaluated for anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.
Direct Coombs test returns strictly negative, ruling out autoimmune hemolytic anemias.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Peripheral blood smear reveals normocytic or macrocytic anemia with prominent spiculated echinocytes ("blister cells") and polychromasia.
Enzymatic assay of red blood cell hemolysate demonstrates severely reduced activity of the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase.
Management is primarily supportive with red blood cell transfusions, splenectomy in severe cases, and monitoring for iron overload.
An adult male visits the emergency department complaining of fatigue, dark urine, and jaundice.
Laboratory testing shows hemolytic anemia, and elevated indirect bilirubin, high LDH, and low haptoglobin during acute hemolytic anemia episodes.
History reveals he was recently prescribed a course of sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim.
Peripheral blood smear demonstrates normocytic hemolytic anemia with pathognomonic denatured hemoglobin aggregates attached to red blood cell membranes (Heinz bodies) and bite cells.
Pathophysiology involves an X-linked recessive enzymatic defect impairing the production of NADPH required to neutralize oxidative stress.
Diagnosis is confirmed by quantitative G6PD enzyme assay, though testing should be delayed weeks after an acute hemolytic crisis.
A young child is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of recurrent infections, and partial oculocutaneous albinism.
Physical examination reveals silvery hair, pale skin, photophobia, and progressive neurological deficits, including peripheral neuropathy and ataxia.
Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow examination reveal pathognomonic giant azurophilic granules within neutrophils and leukocyte precursors.
Patients are at extreme risk for developing an aggressive, fatal "accelerated phase" characterized by lymphohistiocytic infiltration of visceral organs.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the LYST (CHS1) gene encoding a lysosomal trafficking regulator protein.
A male infant is evaluated for recurrent infections, persistent bloody diarrhea.
Complete blood count demonstrates severe thrombocytopenia with characteristically small platelets (microthrombocytopenia).
Family history indicates an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern affecting male relatives.
Physical examination reveals extensive purpura, eczema across the skin folds, and recurrent otitis media.
Immunological evaluation reveals combined immunodeficiency with low IgM levels, variable IgG, and elevated IgA and IgE.
Genetic testing finds a mutation in an X-linked gene at Xp11 that encodes a regulator of actin cytoskeleton reorganization in blood cells.
A young boy is brought to the pediatric clinic presenting with recurrent infections.
Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, persistent lymphadenopathy, and chronic eczematous skin dermatitis.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates chronic normocytic anemia and marked leukocytosis.

Pathophysiology involves defective phagocytic respiratory burst due to failure to produce superoxide radicals, and infections caused by catalase-positive organisms like Staphylococcus aureus and Serratia marcescens.
Diagnostic screening using the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry assay or nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test demonstrates absent fluorescent oxidation.
Genetic testing confirms X-linked (CYBB gene) or autosomal recessive mutations affecting the NADPH oxidase complex.
A newborn infant is evaluated for delayed separation of the umbilical cord stump, persisting beyond three weeks, accompanied by severe omphalitis.
Physical examination reveals recurrent skin infections, deep necrotic ulcers, and severe periodontitis without any pus formation (lack of neutrophils at infection sites).
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates profound peripheral blood leukocytosis with white blood cell counts exceeding 50,000/microliter, consisting predominantly of mature neutrophils.
Pathophysiology involves failure of leukocyte adhesion and migration across vascular endothelial walls.
Flow cytometry confirms absent surface expression of CD18 (beta-2 integrin).
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the ITGB2 gene.
An infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for recurrent infections, persistent diarrhea, and failure to thrive.
Complete blood count demonstrates profound lymphopenia with normal red blood cell and platelet counts.
Physical examination reveals complete absence of lymphoid tissue, absent tonsils, and absence of thymic shadow on chest radiography.
Immunological workup confirms absent T-cell function and absent or defective B-cell and NK-cell numbers depending on the specific genetic subtype.
Pathophysiology involves profound failure of adaptive immunity, representing a pediatric medical emergency requiring isolation and stem cell transplantation.
Genetic testing identifies a mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain of cytokine receptors.
A child is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of recurrent infections and severe eczema.
Pathophysiology involves impaired differentiation of T-helper 17 (Th17) cells, leading to defective neutrophil recruitment to sites of infection.
Physical examination reveals distinctive coarse facial features, a prominent broad nasal bridge, high arched palate, and retained primary teeth.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates extreme elevations of serum IgE levels exceeding 2,000 IU/ml and peripheral eosinophilia.
Family history indicates an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms heterozygous dominant-negative mutations in the STAT3 gene.
A young child is brought to the clinic presenting with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease).
Physical examination reveals patchy hair loss (alopecia areata), vitiligo, dental enamel hypoplasia, and nail dystrophy.
Endocrine evaluation confirms multiple autoimmune glandular failures occurring progressively over childhood and adolescence.
Pathophysiology involves failure of central immune tolerance and negative thymic selection.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene on chromosome 21q22.3.
A newborn infant identified through routine expanded newborn screening is evaluated for classic amino acid metabolism disorder.
Untreated infants develop profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, musty "mousy" body odor, and hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes.
Physical examination reveals generalized eczema and unprovoked seizures.
Laboratory workup confirms markedly elevated serum phenylalanine levels alongside low tyrosine concentrations.
Pathophysiology involves impaired conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine due to deficient hepatic enzyme activity.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the PAH gene encoding phenylalanine hydroxylase, treated successfully with early dietary phenylalanine restriction.
An adult patient visits the clinic complaining of dark black urine upon standing and bluish-black discoloration of the sclerae and ear cartilage (ochronosis).
Patient reports experiencing chronic, severe degenerative arthritis affecting the spine and large joints, with joint fluid staining dark brown.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated homogentisic acid in urine samples, which turns jet-black upon alkalinization or exposure to air.
Pathophysiology involves deficient catabolism of tyrosine and phenylalanine, leading to tissue accumulation of homogentisic acid polymers.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the HGD gene encoding homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase.
A child is evaluated for tall stature, developmental delay.
Physical examination reveals long slender limbs, arachnodactyly, scoliosis, and skeletal deformities resembling Marfan syndrome.
Unlike Marfan syndrome, patients exhibit high risk for severe thromboembolic events (strokes, pulmonary emboli) and intellectual disability.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates elevated plasma homocysteine and methionine levels, alongside positive urinary cyanide-nitroprusside screening.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the CBS gene encoding cystathionine beta-synthase.
A neonate born to healthy parents develops lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, and neurologic deterioration within the first week of life.
Nursing staff notes a distinctive, sweet, maple syrup or burnt sugar odor emanating from the infant's earwax and urine.
Neurological examination reveals alternating periods of hypertonia (opisthotonos) and flaccidity, leading rapidly to seizures, coma, and respiratory failure.
Laboratory workup demonstrates marked metabolic ketoacidosis with elevated plasma branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine).
Pathophysiology involves deficient activity of the mitochondrial branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in BCKDHA, BCKDHB, or DBT genes, requiring lifelong specialized synthetic amino acid diets.
A 2-month-old infant presents with progressive microcephaly, irritability, intermittent sterile pyrexias, and global developmental stagnation following an apparently normal birth.
Physical examination reveals spastic diplegia, hyperreflexia, axial hypotonia, and characteristic bilateral chilblain-like purple-red skin lesions localized on the fingers, toes, and earlobes.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals marked chronic lymphocytosis and a profoundly elevated baseline interferon-alpha (IFN-α) activity level (the "interferon signature").
Cranial CT scan demonstrates extensive, symmetric bilateral calcifications of the basal ganglia and cerebral white matter.
Brain MRI reveals diffuse white matter signal abnormalities, cerebral atrophy, and delayed myelination without signs of congenital perinatal infection.
Molecular genetic panel confirms biallelic mutations in one of the causal ribonuclease H2 complex genes (such as RNASEH2B), establishing the severe autoinflammatory encephalopathy.
A male infant is evaluated for progressive neurological deterioration, hypotonia, and peculiar kinky, depigmented hair starting around two months of age.
Physical examination reveals pudgy, cherubic facies, pale skin, severe developmental delay, and severe motor regression.
Microscopic examination of scalp hair reveals twisted hair shafts ("pili torti") and trichopoliodystrophy.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates profoundly low serum copper and ceruloplasmin levels due to impaired intestinal copper absorption and systemic trapping.
Family history indicates an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern affecting male relatives.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the ATP7A gene encoding a copper-transporting P-type ATPase.
An infant is evaluated at six months of age for progressive loss of developmental milestones, lethargy.
Ophthalmologic fundoscopic examination reveals pathognomonic cherry-red spots at the fovea centralis surrounded by pale surrounding ganglion cell layers.
Physical examination reveals progressive hypotonia progressing to spasticity, macrocephaly, and seizures and an exaggerated startle response to sudden loud noises (hyperacusis).
Laboratory enzymatic assay demonstrates absent activity of hexosaminidase A in leukocytes or serum.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern with high carrier frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish populations.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the HEXA gene on chromosome 15q23, leading to fatal neurodegeneration in early childhood.
A child or adolescent is evaluated for progressive ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, and unexplained vertical supranuclear gaze palsy.
Physical examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly, cognitive decline, and progressive difficulty moving eyes in the vertical plane.
Bone marrow aspirate reveals large lipid-laden foam cells, while filipin staining of skin fibroblasts shows abnormal intracellular cholesterol accumulation.
Pathophysiology involves defective intracellular cholesterol and glycosphingolipid trafficking.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms biallelic mutations in a gene for lysosomal cholesterol transport.
An adult patient visits the hematology clinic complaining of chronic fatigue, easy bruising, and progressive abdominal distension.
Physical examination reveals splenomegaly and hepatomegaly without primary neurological involvement.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates pancytopenia, elevated serum acid phosphatase, and high chitotriosidase levels.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals pathognomonic large lipid-engorged macrophages with crumpled tissue paper-like cytoplasm (Gaucher cells).
Enzymatic assay confirms deficient activity of lysosomal beta-glucocerebrosidase.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the GBA gene, treated successfully with enzyme replacement therapy.

A 3-year-old female toddler is brought by her parents for evaluation due to complete cessation of spoken language, and severe social withdrawal following normal early development up to 15 months of age.

Physical examination reveals deceleration of head growth leading to acquired microcephaly, profound gait ataxia, and characteristic stereotypic midline hand movements (such as compulsive hand-wringing, clapping, or mouthing).
Neurological evaluation notes severe apraxia, autistic-like social communication deficits, and intermittent breathing irregularities during wakefulness (episodic hyperventilation and breath-holding).
Skeletal survey reveals secondary osteopenia, while metabolic screening and brain structural MRI are structurally unremarkable or show mild nonspecific atrophy.
Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrates generalized background slowing, loss of normal sleep rhythms, and intermittent epileptiform discharges originating from the central and frontal regions.
Molecular genetic testing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the X-linked MECP2 (Methyl-CpG-binding protein 2) gene, confirming the classic neurodevelopmental disorder.
An infant is evaluated for coarse facial features, skeletal deformities, and developmental delay appearing in the first year of life.
Physical examination reveals a large head, depressed nasal bridge, protruding tongue, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, and stiff joints.
Skeletal survey demonstrates characteristic "dysostosis multiplex" featuring thickened ribs, bullet-shaped vertebral bodies, and short metacarpals.
Urinary screening reveals massive excretion of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycans.
Enzymatic assay confirms deficient activity of alpha-L-iduronidase.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the IDUA gene, treated with stem cell transplantation or enzyme replacement.
A young male child is evaluated for progressive coarse facial features, skeletal dysplasia, and joint stiffness.
Physical examination reveals prominent coarse facies, macrocephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, and widespread skin papules (dermal melanocytosis), but notably lacks corneal clouding.
Family history reveals X-linked recessive inheritance affecting male maternal relatives.
Urinary assay confirms elevated urinary dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate excretion.
Enzymatic assay demonstrates deficient activity of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase (I2S).
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the IDS gene on the X chromosome.

disease: Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (von Gierke Disease)
clues: An infant is brought to the pediatric clinic for evaluation of massive hepatomegaly.
Physical examination reveals prominent abdominal distension due to massive hepatomegaly, short stature, and thin extremities.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates severe fasting hypoglycemia accompanied by lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Pathophysiology involves defective hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Family history indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the G6PC gene encoding glucose-6-phosphatase.

disease: Glycogen Storage Disease Type II (Pompe Disease)
clues: An infant is evaluated in the neonatal intensive care unit for profound generalized muscle hypotonia ("floppy baby"), feeding difficulties.
Physical examination reveals massive cardiomegaly with progressive heart failure and respiratory distress, also macroglossia.
Electrocardiogram demonstrates characteristically shortened PR intervals and massive QRS voltage voltages.
Muscle biopsy reveals vacuolar myopathy with massive intracellular glycogen accumulation within lysosomes.
Enzymatic assay demonstrates deficient activity of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (acid maltase).
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the GAA gene, treated successfully with enzyme replacement therapy.

disease: Glycogen Storage Disease Type III (Cori Disease / Forbes Disease)
clues: A child is evaluated for hepatomegaly, and growth retardation.
Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly that tends to improve and regress significantly after puberty.
Laboratory evaluation reveals normal blood lactate and uric acid levels, but demonstrates fasting ketosis.
Skeletal muscle involvement leads to progressive myopathy and muscle weakness.
Enzymatic assay confirms deficient activity of the glycogen debranching enzyme (amylo-1,6-glucosidase).
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the AGL gene.

disease: Glycogen Storage Disease Type V (McArdle Disease)
clues: An adult patient visits the neurology clinic complaining of painful muscle cramps, fatigue, and stiffness occurring shortly after beginning strenuous exercise.
flat venous lactate curve during ischemic forearm exercise testing due to failure of lactate production.
Patient reports experiencing the "second wind" phenomenon, where resting briefly during exercise relieves symptoms and allows activity to resume.
Laboratory evaluation demonstrates that serum creatine kinase levels are chronically elevated with episodes of myoglobinuria and dark urine following heavy exertion.
Enzymatic assay confirms deficient activity of muscle glycogen phosphorylase.
Genetic testing confirms autosomal recessive mutations in the PYGM gene.
A male infant is evaluated for developmental delay, and bizarre compulsive self-injurious behavior involving biting of the lips and fingers.
Physical examination reveals hyperreflexia, dystonia, and massive overproduction of uric acid leading to orange crystals in diapers.
Laboratory workup reveals hyperuricemia, marked hyperuricosuria, and gouty arthritis.
Family history indicates an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern affecting male relatives.
Enzymatic assay demonstrates complete absence of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) activity.
Genetic testing confirms mutations in the HPRT1 gene on the X chromosome, managed with allopurinol and behavioral restraints.
A 4-year-old girl is brought to the pediatric rheumatology clinic due to recurring fevers, and persistent swelling in both wrists.
Physical examination shows non-tender boggy tenosynovitis of the wrists and ankles, diffuse hyperpigmented erythematous papules on the trunk, and anterior uveitis on slit-lamp exam.
Inflammatory markers show significantly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), while ANA and rheumatoid factor are negative.
Plain radiographs of the affected joints demonstrate periarticular osteopenia and joint space widening without focal bone erosions.
Skin biopsy of a papule reveals non-caseating granulomatous dermatitis with prominent multinucleated giant cells.
Genetic testing reveals a gain-of-function missense mutation in the NOD2 (CARD15) gene, establishing the diagnosis.
A 19-year-old college student presents to the urgent care clinic with a 3-day history of sore throat, painful swallowing, and fever.
Physical examination shows tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, hyperemic pharyngeal mucosa, and enlarged tonsils coated with purulent exudate.
Temperature is recorded at 38.8°C (101.8°F), while respiratory exam is clear without cough or rhinorrhea.
Rapid Antigen Detection Test (RADT) from a throat swab returns positive for Group A Streptococcus.
Throat swab culture confirms heavy growth of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus).
Prompt symptomatic relief and resolution occur following a 10-day course of oral Penicillin V.
A 5-year-old child is evaluated for global developmental delay, speech articulation difficulties, and severe behavioral problems including self-injurious acts and compulsive self-hug behaviors.
Physical examination reveals characteristic facial dysmorphism including a square-shaped face, deep-set eyes, midface hypoplasia, a prominent downturned "tented" upper lip, and short stature.

Sleep study (polysomnography) uncovers a severely disrupted sleep architecture driven by inverted circadian melatonin secretion, characterized by daytime somnolence and frequent night and early-morning waking.
Behavioral observation notes extreme emotional lability, severe temper tantrums, and a pathognomonic compulsive need for knuckle-biting and pulling out fingernails (onychotillomania).
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or chromosomal microarray analysis detects a microdeletion on the short arm of chromosome 17 at band p11.2 (17p11.2 deletion).
Molecular genetic confirmation reveals hemizygosity or mutation involving the RAI1 (Retinoic acid-induced 1) gene within the deleted region, establishing the multisystem genomic disorder.
A 62-year-old man presents to the general surgery clinic after noticing a bulge in his right groin.
Physical examination reveals a soft, non-tender mass in the right inguinal region superior to the inguinal ligament.
The mass increases in size when the patient stands up or coughs (positive cough impulse) and completely disappears when he lies supine.
Gentle manual pressure easily reduces the protrusion back into the abdominal cavity without producing discomfort.
High-resolution groin ultrasound confirms the presence of a peritoneal sac containing omentum protruding through the deep internal ring.
Elective repair (herniorrhaphy with mesh placement) restores normal abdominal wall architecture without complications.
A 42-year-old woman presents with rapid-onset bilateral eye redness, deep eye pain, vertigo, and sudden hearing loss over the past 3 weeks.
Physical examination demonstrates bilateral deep perilimbal corneal injection, ataxia, and severe bilateral sensorineural hearing loss on audiometric testing.
Slit-lamp exam reveals non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis with diffuse stromal infiltrates.
Inflammatory markers are elevated with an ESR of 84 mm/hr, while ANA, ANCA, RF, and treponemal serologies are all negative.
High-resolution MRI of the inner ear shows soft-tissue enhancement within the membranous labyrinth and vestibule.
The clinical constellation of non-syphilitic interstitial keratitis, vestibuloauditory dysfunction, and systemic vasculitic features confirms the diagnosis.
A 52-year-old man presents with sudden, severe, continuous abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea over the past 24 hours.
Laboratory testing shows elevated serum lactate (5.8 mmol/L) and severe leukocytosis.
He reports a history of essential thrombocythemia.
Physical examination reveals severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical exam findings, progressing to abdominal distension and reduced bowel sounds.
Abdominal ultrasound with Doppler demonstrates absent venous flow within the main trunk of the superior mesenteric vein.
Emergency exploratory laparotomy confirms ischemic bowel loops caused by SMV occlusion, establishing the diagnosis.
A 22-year-old male presents to the clinic concerned about patches of lighter skin on his upper chest and back.
Physical examination displays multiple hyper- and hypopigmented macules with fine, superficial scaling that coalesce across the upper trunk.
Gentle scraping of the scale yields microscopic visualization of short, thick hyphae mixed with round yeast cells ("spaghetti and meatballs" appearance).
Wood's lamp examination of the affected torso shows a subtle yellow-orange fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
Fungal organism is identified as overgrowth of the lipophilic commensal yeast Malassezia globosa.
Complete clearance of skin scaling occurs following topical treatment with ketoconazole 2% shampoo.
A 28-year-old school teacher presents with a persistent cough lasting for 3 weeks.
Physical examination between coughing spells is completely normal, but an episode in the clinic culminates in a high-pitched inspiratory sound and post-tussive vomiting.
Laboratory testing shows prominent leukocytosis with absolute lymphocytosis despite a lack of significant fever.
Nasopharyngeal swab PCR testing detects DNA of the causative organism, confirming a toxin-mediated respiratory infection.
Nasopharyngeal culture on Regan-Lowe charcoal agar isolates small, gram-negative coccobacilli.
Treatment with oral azithromycin reduces infectivity, and household contacts receive post-exposure macrolide prophylaxis.
A 31-year-old avid backpacker presents with 2 weeks of watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence.
Physical examination reveals abdominal distension and diffuse mild abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs.
Stool microscopy demonstrates binucleated, flagellated trophozoites with a teardrop shape and a ventral sucking disk.
Stool antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA) tests positive for Giardia duodenalis specific proteins.
Stool examination shows absence of fecal leukocytes, blood, or mucus, confirming non-invasive malabsorptive enteritis.
Rapid eradication of gastrointestinal symptoms follows a 5-day course of oral metronidazole.
A 71-year-old woman presents with sudden onset of severe right knee swelling, redness, and excruciating pain that began overnight.
Physical examination reveals a warm, erythematous right knee joint with a large suprapatellar effusion and severely restricted range of motion.
Arthrocentesis yields turbid synovial fluid with a leukocyte count of 32,000/µL with neutrophil predominance.
Polarized light microscopy of joint fluid identifies weakly positively birefringent, rhomboid-shaped intra- and extracellular crystals.
Plain X-rays of the knee demonstrate chondrocalcinosis, visible as linear calcification of the articular hyaline cartilage and meniscus.
Symptomatic improvement is rapidly achieved with intra-articular corticosteroid injection and oral NSAID therapy.
A 32-year-old heavy cigarette smoker presents with severe resting pain in his bilateral feet and fingers, accompanied by small painful ulcerations on his fingertips.
Physical examination shows absent dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, ischemic digital ulcers, and superficial migratory thrombophlebitis in the legs.
Laboratory evaluation shows normal ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, anti-CCP, and normal hypercoagulability panel.
Non-invasive arterial Doppler ultrasound confirms distal infrapopliteal segmental occlusive arterial disease with normal proximal vessels.
Catheter angiography demonstrates segmental occlusion of small and medium-sized arteries with a characteristic "corkscrew" collateral vessel pattern.
Complete cessation of tobacco product use halts disease progression and prevents limb amputation.
A 58-year-old man presents complaining of severe generalized itching, accompanied by frequent headaches and dizziness.
Physical examination reveals a ruddy cyanotic facial complexion, engorged retinal veins on fundoscopy, and palpable splenomegaly 4 cm below the costal margin.
Complete blood count demonstrates Hb 19.8 g/dL, Hematocrit 61%, WBC 14,200/µL, and Platelets 550,000/µL.
Serum erythropoietin (EPO) level is significantly suppressed below the normal reference range.
Bone marrow biopsy reveals hypercellularity with trilineage myeloproliferation (panmyelosis).
Molecular analysis demonstrates the presence of the JAK2 V617F somatic mutation in exon 14, establishing the myeloproliferative neoplasm.
A 42-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of diaphoresis, confusion, blurred vision, and tremor that occur after fasting or exercising.
Physical examination during an active symptomatic episode reveals tachycardia, diaphoresis, and altered mental status that rapidly resolves upon administration of oral glucose (Whipple triad).
Laboratory testing during a 72-hour supervised fast demonstrates serum glucose 38 mg/dL, elevated serum insulin (18 µIU/mL), elevated C-peptide, and negative sulfonylurea screen.
Abdominal multiphase contrast-enhanced CT shows a hypervascular 1.5 cm nodule in the body of the pancreas.
Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) confirms a well-demarcated hypoechoic lesion in the pancreatic parenchyma with fine-needle aspiration showing neuroendocrine histology.
Surgical enucleation of the benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor results in permanent cure of hypoglycemia.
A 29-year-old woman presents with the encephalopathy, sudden low-frequency hearing loss, and dark spots in her visual field.
Physical examination shows sensorineural hearing loss, gait ataxia, confusion, and multiple branch retinal artery occlusions on fundoscopy.
Fluorescein angiography displays multifocal branch retinal artery occlusions with characteristic hyperfluorescence of the arterial wall (Gass plaques).
Audiometry confirms low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally.
Brain MRI reveals classic central "snowball" lesions in the corpus callosum on T2/FLAIR sequences along with leptomeningeal enhancement.
Immune-mediated microvascular endotheliopathy of the brain, retina, and inner ear is treated aggressively with high-dose IV corticosteroids and IVIG.
A 35-year-old male presents with a painless, slowly enlarging mass in his right neck over the past year, accompanied by mild fatigue.
Physical examination discloses a firm, non-tender 5 cm solitary cervical lymph node mass without generalized lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.
Laboratory studies show mild microcytic anemia and mild elevation of serum IL-6, with negative HIV and HHV-8 testing.
Contrast CT neck shows a solitary, intensely hypervascular lymph node mass in the anterior cervical chain.
Excisional biopsy of the mass demonstrates regressed germinal centers with concentric "onion-skin" mantles of small lymphocytes and penetrated hyalinized vessels ("lollipop lesion").
Complete surgical excision of the solitary mass results in curative resolution of all pathological and clinical manifestations.

A 64-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife due to subacute memory loss, spatial disorientation, and brief, frequent jerking movements of his right arm and right side of his face occurring up to 50 times a day.
Physical examination reveals cognitive impairment with prominent short-term memory deficits, executive dysfunction, and pathognomonic faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS).
Serum laboratory evaluation shows marked hyponatremia (122 mEq/L) secondary to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH).
Electroencephalography (EEG) records brief, high-amplitude slow-wave paroxysms preceding the clinical motor jerks without typical epileptiform discharges.
Brain MRI displays T2/FLAIR hyperintensity localized to the bilateral medial temporal lobes and basal ganglia.
Serum and CSF antibody testing confirms positive IgG autoantibodies against Leucine-Rich Glioma-Inactivated 1 (LGI1).

disease: PAPA Syndrome (Pyogenic Arthritis, Pyoderma Gangrenosum, and Acne)
clues: A 16-year-old male presents with severe, recurrent joint swelling, widespread ulcerative skin lesions, and nodulocystic facial acne that has progressively worsened since early childhood.
Physical examination reveals destructive sterile inflammatory arthritis of the ankles and knees, along with large cribriform-scarred ulcerative skin plaques consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum.
Synovial fluid aspiration from the swollen knee yields purulent material that is completely sterile on bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures.
Laboratory studies demonstrate marked elevation of ESR, CRP, and serum amyloid A, with marked neutrophilic leukocytosis.
Histopathology of a skin lesion biopsy reveals a dense dermal infiltrate predominantly composed of mature neutrophils with sterile necrosis.
Genetic sequencing identifies a heterozygous missense mutation in the PSTPIP1 gene on chromosome 15q24, confirming the autoinflammatory diagnosis.
A 45-year-old obese male with type 2 diabetes presents with a non-itchy reddish-brown rash in both groins and axillae that has been present for several months.
Physical examination reveals well-demarcated, dry, reddish-brown macular patches with fine scaling located in the intertriginous folds.
Wood’s lamp examination of the affected skin folds demonstrates a brilliant coral-red fluorescence under ultraviolet light.
Skin scrapings evaluated under potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation show no fungal elements or hyphae.
Gram stain of the scale demonstrates small, pleomorphic gram-positive rods, identifying overgrowth of Corynebacterium minutissimum.
Rapid resolution of the intertriginous rash occurs following topical clindamycin lotion application.
A 78-year-old woman is found very drowsy at home on a cold winter morning by her neighbour.
Over recent weeks she had become slow, forgetful, constipated, and always felt cold.
She stopped taking a daily tablet a few months ago and recently started a sedative for sleep.
Her temperature is 33.5 °C, her heart rate is 44 bpm, and her breathing is slow and shallow.
Her face and hands are puffy, her skin is dry, her ankle reflexes relax slowly, and her sodium is low.
TSH is very high and free T4 very low; she receives IV levothyroxine with IV hydrocortisone in intensive care.
A 34-year-old traveler returning from Central America presents with 3 weeks of persistent watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and weight loss.
Physical examination reveals abdominal distension with diffuse mild tenderness but no peritoneal signs or fever.
Stool wet mount examination under phase-contrast microscopy reveals spherical, unsporulated oocysts measuring 8–10 micrometers in diameter.
Modified Ziehl-Neelsen (acid-fast) staining of stool demonstrates variably staining, bright pink-to-red round oocysts.
Ultraviolet fluorescence microscopy of the stool smear reveals bright blue autofluorescence of the oocysts under UV light excitation.
Symptoms completely resolve following a 7-day course of oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX).
A 42-year-old female presents with sudden, severe right shoulder pain that woke her from sleep, preventing any movement of her right arm.
Physical examination shows exquisite tenderness over the anterior aspect of the greater tuberosity with severe restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement.
Serum inflammatory markers (ESR and CRP) and leukocyte count are within normal reference ranges.
Plain shoulder radiography reveals a dense, amorphous, well-circumscribed radiopaque deposit within the supraspinatus tendon.
Musculoskeletal ultrasound displays a hyperechoic focus with acoustic shadowing situated within the substance of the rotator cuff tendon.
Therapeutic ultrasound-guided barbotage (lavage) with intra-bursal corticosteroid injection yields immediate, dramatic pain relief.
A 62-year-old male smoker presents with episodic left arm fatigue, hand claudication, dizziness, and double vision.
Auscultation over the left supraclavicular fossa reveals a high-pitched arterial bruit.
He mentioned that the symptoms occur exclusively while exercising his left arm.
Physical examination reveals a 30 mmHg systolic blood pressure difference between the arms (right > left) and a significantly diminished left radial pulse.
CT angiography of the chest confirms severe stenosis at the proximal origin of the left subclavian artery, proximal to the origin of the left vertebral artery.
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stent placement across the subclavian artery lesion completely restores antegrade vertebral flow and relieves neurological symptoms.
A 50-year-old woman presents with severe, continuous, watery diarrhea for 2 months that persists even during prolonged fasting.
Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, muscle weakness, and abdominal distension.
Serum chemistry demonstrates severe hypokalemia (2.1 mEq/L), hypochlorhydria, and metabolic acidosis with normal gastrin and serotonin levels.
Fasting plasma Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) level is markedly elevated at >500 pg/mL (normal <75 pg/mL).
Abdominal contrast CT reveals a 4 cm hypervascular tumor located in the tail of the pancreas.
Administration of octreotide rapidly stops the watery diarrhea, and subsequent surgical resection cures the neuroendocrine tumor.
A 54-year-old woman presents for routine blood work and reports persistent burning pain in her toes and fingers along with transient visual disturbances.
Physical examination reveals warm, red, exquisitely tender digital pads in hands and feet, with mild splenomegaly noted on abdominal palpation.
Routine complete blood count reveals an isolated, sustained platelet count of 1,150,000/µL with normal hemoglobin and leukocyte counts.
Peripheral blood smear shows massive numbers of platelets with significant size variation and large megakaryocyte fragments, but no teardrop cells.
Bone marrow biopsy demonstrates marked megakaryocytic hypercellularity with prominent large, mature megakaryocytes in hyperlobated clusters without collagen fibrosis.
Molecular testing detects a driver mutation in the CALR (Calreticulin) gene in exon 9, establishing the myeloproliferative neoplasm.
A 5-day-old male infant presents with progressive lethargy, poor feeding, severe vomiting, and a distinct odor emanating from his skin and diapers.
Physical examination shows a somnolent infant with axial hypotonia, hyperreflexia, and episodic muscular twitching.
Laboratory testing reveals severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis, marked hyperammonemia (380 µmol/L), and severe ketonuria.
Urine organic acid analysis by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry reveals massive excretion of isovalerylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid.
Tandem mass spectrometry newborn screening card analysis shows significantly elevated isovalerylcarnitine (C5) levels.
Molecular genetic testing identifies biallelic pathogenic mutations in the IVD gene encoding isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase.
A 44-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of severe bilateral ear pain, redness, and swelling that spare the non-cartilaginous earlobes.
Physical examination demonstrates violaceous erythema and exquisite tenderness of the bilateral auricular cartilage with lobule sparing, alongside a saddle-nose deformity.
Audiometric testing displays sensorineural hearing loss, while slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral episcleritis.
Inspiratory/expiratory dynamic CT scan of the chest demonstrates diffuse thickening and calcification of the anterior cartilaginous tracheal rings with sparing of the posterior membranous wall.
Biopsy of affected ear cartilage demonstrates destruction of the cartilaginous matrix with a dense perichondrial lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrate.
High-dose systemic immunosuppression with corticosteroids and methotrexate induces disease remission and prevents airway collapse.
A 59-year-old male presents with recurrent bacterial skin infections, fatigue, and persistent low-grade fevers.
Physical examination reveals moderate splenomegaly, rheumatoid hand deformities, and absence of peripheral lymphadenopathy.
Complete blood count demonstrates severe isolated absolute neutropenia (ANC 300/µL) with a modest overall lymphocytosis.
Peripheral blood smear reveals medium-to-large lymphocytes containing abundant pale blue cytoplasm with prominent azurophilic cytoplasmic granules.
Flow cytometry of peripheral blood displays a clonal population of mature T-cells expressing CD3+, CD8+, CD57+, and TCR alpha-beta markers.
Next-generation sequencing detects a somatic hotspot mutation in the STAT3 gene (specifically Y640F), confirming LGL leukemia.
A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with three days of high fever and fussiness.
His parents describe a hacking cough, a runny nose, and red, watery eyes that are sensitive to light.
The family recently returned from abroad, and the boy's vaccinations were never completed.
Inside the cheeks, small bluish-white spots on a red background are seen opposite the lower molars.
A blotchy red rash starts at the hairline behind the ears and spreads down over the trunk and limbs.
Serum IgM against the paramyxovirus is positive; he receives vitamin A and supportive care, and the case is reported to public health.
A 62-year-old man is rushed to the emergency department with sudden, severe chest pain that began while lifting a box.
He describes the pain as tearing, reaching its worst at onset and moving to the area between his shoulder blades.
He has long-standing hypertension that he controls poorly and smokes a pack a day.
Blood pressure is 182/96 mmHg in the right arm but only 138/80 mmHg in the left arm.
A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and a soft early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border.
CT angiography shows an intimal flap in the ascending aorta, and he is taken for emergency surgical repair.
A 64-year-old man visits his doctor because climbing stairs and rising from a chair have become harder over several months.
He also notices a dry mouth, constipation, and new erectile dysfunction.
He has a 50 pack-year smoking history and has recently lost weight without trying.
Hip and shoulder muscles are weak and reflexes are reduced, yet after a short burst of exercise both strength and reflexes briefly improve.
Repetitive nerve stimulation at high frequency shows a marked increase in muscle response amplitude.
Antibodies against P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels are found, and a chest CT reveals a small cell lung carcinoma.
A 24-year-old man sees an eye doctor because he struggles to see at night and keeps bumping into things in dim light.
Over the past year he has also lost his sense of smell and noticed numbness in both feet.
Examination shows dry, scaly skin, shortened fourth toes, and an unsteady gait with absent ankle reflexes.
Fundoscopy reveals retinitis pigmentosa, and a hearing test shows sensorineural hearing loss.
Plasma testing reveals a markedly raised phytanic acid level.
Genetic testing confirms an autosomal recessive PHYH mutation, and he begins a diet free of dairy, ruminant fats, and fatty fish.
A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her partner because she has become restless and confused over the evening.
She is sweating heavily, has diarrhea, and keeps saying she feels shaky and cannot sit still.
She takes sertraline for depression and started tramadol two days ago for back pain.
She has a temperature of 38.9 °C, a heart rate of 128 bpm, and dilated pupils.
The neurological exam shows hyperreflexia and inducible clonus that is most marked in the legs.
Both drugs are stopped and she improves with benzodiazepines, cooling, and cyproheptadine.
A 45-year-old woman comes to clinic after several sudden attacks of spinning dizziness over the past two months.
Each attack lasts a few hours and leaves her nauseated, so she has to lie still until it passes.
Before each attack, her right ear feels full and blocked.
She hears a low roaring sound in the same ear, which gets louder during attacks.
An audiogram shows low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss in the right ear that varies between visits.
Her symptoms improve on a low-salt diet with a diuretic, and she is given a short-term antiemetic for attacks.
A 27-year-old woman visits her doctor about headaches that keep coming back every few weeks.
Each headache builds over an hour, throbs on one side of her head, and lasts most of the day.
During attacks she feels sick, vomits, and has to lie in a dark, quiet room.
About twenty minutes before the pain, she sees zigzag flashing lines that spread across her vision and then fade.
Her mother had similar headaches, and attacks often come around her period or after missed sleep.
Her neurological exam is normal; a triptan at onset ends her attacks, and a headache diary is started.
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic with a mild fever and tiredness for one day.
Her parents say she has been scratching all night and is very grumpy.
Several children in her kindergarten class have been off sick with spots this month.
Itchy red spots appeared first on her chest and back and then spread to her face and scalp.
The spots turn into small clear blisters like dewdrops on a red base, with new crops appearing beside crusted older ones.
She is kept home until all lesions crust over and is given calamine lotion and paracetamol, avoiding aspirin.
A 10-month-old baby is brought to the clinic after three days of very high fever.
Despite temperatures near 40 °C, the baby has been feeding and playing fairly normally between fever spikes.
The parents were frightened because the baby had a brief febrile seizure on the second day.
This morning the fever suddenly disappeared.
A few hours later, small pink spots appeared on the trunk and neck that fade when pressed and do not itch.
The rash fades within two days; it is caused by human herpesvirus 6, and only reassurance is needed.
A 17-year-old student visits the clinic feeling exhausted for over a week.
He has a fever and a very sore throat that makes swallowing painful.
He recently started dating someone new at school.
His tonsils are large with a grey-white coating, and the lymph nodes at the back of his neck are swollen and tender.
His spleen tip can be felt below the left rib cage, and his blood film shows many atypical lymphocytes.
A heterophile antibody (Monospot) test is positive, and he is told to avoid contact sports for several weeks.
A 72-year-old man tells his doctor that his eyesight has slowly worsened over the past two years.
He finds reading harder and has stopped driving at night.
He has type 2 diabetes and used steroid inhalers for many years.
He complains that headlights and the sun cause bright glare and halos.
There is no pain or redness, but colours look faded and yellowish to him.
Slit-lamp exam shows a cloudy lens, and he is booked for lens removal with an artificial lens implant.
A 22-year-old university swimmer comes to the clinic about an itchy foot.
The itching is worse at night and after he takes off his trainers.
He uses the shared showers at the pool every day without sandals.
The skin between his fourth and fifth toes is white, soggy, and peeling, with small cracks.
A skin scraping examined with potassium hydroxide shows branching fungal hyphae.
He is treated with a topical antifungal cream and told to keep his feet dry and wear sandals in shared showers.
A 15-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother because he has become shy and avoids school photos.
He says the problem started about a year ago and is worse before exams.
His father had a similar problem as a teenager that left some scars.
His forehead, nose, and chin have many blackheads and whiteheads.
There are also red bumps and pus-filled spots on his cheeks and upper back.
He starts topical benzoyl peroxide with a retinoid, and oral doxycycline is added for the inflamed spots.
A 38-year-old office worker visits his doctor feeling embarrassed about a problem in the bathroom.
He has had constipation for months and often strains on the toilet.
He eats little fibre and sits at his desk most of the day.
He notices bright red blood on the toilet paper and dripping into the bowl after stools, without pain.
He also feels a soft lump at the anus after straining that slips back in on its own.
Anoscopy shows swollen vascular cushions above the dentate line; he is advised more fibre and water, and banding is offered.
A 19-year-old student comes in because eating has become painful.
She says this happens a few times a year, especially during exam weeks.
She has no fever and feels otherwise well.
Inside her lower lip there are two small round sores.
Each sore is shallow with a yellow-grey base and a red halo, and is very tender to touch.
They heal on their own within ten days; she is given a soothing mouthwash and a topical steroid paste.
A 16-year-old football player comes to the clinic limping.
He says his big toe hurts when he wears his boots and when someone steps on it.
He cuts his nails short and rounds off the corners.
The side of his right big toe is red, swollen, and very tender.
The edge of the nail is digging into the skin fold, with a little pus and overgrown tissue.
The nail edge is removed under local anaesthetic, and he is shown how to cut his nails straight across.
A 4-year-old boy is brought in because of small bumps on his skin that have been there for two months.
The bumps do not hurt but sometimes itch, and more keep appearing.
His older sister had similar bumps last year, and they share bath time.
On his trunk and armpits there are about fifteen firm, smooth, skin-coloured bumps.
Each bump is pearly and dome-shaped with a small dent in the centre.
It is caused by a poxvirus, the bumps usually clear on their own within months, and the family is reassured.
A 7-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her father because she cannot stop scratching her head.
The itch is worst at night and has lasted about three weeks.
A note was sent home from school saying several classmates had the same problem.
There are scratch marks and small red bumps at the back of her neck and behind her ears.
Tiny white specks are firmly stuck to hair shafts close to the scalp and do not brush off like dandruff.
Live insects are seen with a fine-toothed comb, and she is treated with a dimeticone lotion repeated after a week.
A 9-month-old baby is brought in because she cries during nappy changes.
Her mother has been using a new brand of baby wipes, and the baby had diarrhoea last week.
The baby is feeding well and has no fever.
The skin over her buttocks and outer labia is red, shiny, and sore.
The deep skin folds of the groin are spared, and there are no separate satellite spots.
It settles with frequent changes, nappy-free time, and a zinc oxide barrier cream.
Tired parents bring their 6-week-old son to the clinic because of long crying spells.
He cries hard for more than three hours a day, mostly in the late afternoon and evening.
The crying started at two weeks of age and happens on most days of the week.
During spells he goes red in the face, clenches his fists, and pulls his legs up to his tummy.
Between spells he feeds well, is gaining weight normally, and his examination is completely normal.
The parents are reassured that it usually stops by three to four months and given soothing tips and support.
A healthy baby boy born at term two days ago is checked before going home.
His mother noticed a rash this morning and is worried it might be an infection.
He is feeding well, has no fever, and is alert and active.
His chest, back, and thighs have blotchy red patches, some with tiny pale yellow bumps in the middle.
The spots move around, fading in some places and appearing in others within hours, and his palms and soles are spared.
A smear of a bump would show eosinophils; it is harmless and fades within one to two weeks without treatment.
A 26-year-old man comes to the clinic about changes in his skin colour that started a few months ago.
He has no itching or pain, but he feels self-conscious at work.
He has autoimmune thyroid disease, and his aunt has a similar skin condition.
There are sharply outlined, completely white patches around his mouth, eyes, and on the backs of his hands.
Under a Wood's lamp, the patches glow bright chalk-white.
A potent topical steroid or tacrolimus is started, with narrowband UVB phototherapy offered for wider areas.
A 58-year-old man asks his doctor about the look of his toenails.
He says the problem has slowly got worse over two years and makes it hard to cut his nails.
He has diabetes and had athlete's foot several times.
Three of his toenails are thick, crumbly, and yellow-brown.
The nails are lifting from the nail bed, with chalky debris underneath.
Nail clippings show fungal hyphae on microscopy and grow a dermatophyte; he starts oral terbinafine for three months.
A 30-year-old woman visits the clinic about a lump on her eyelid.
She noticed it three weeks ago, and it was a little sore at first but now is not painful.
She has rosacea and often has crusty, irritated eyelids.
On her upper eyelid there is a firm, round, pea-sized lump.
The lump sits away from the lid margin, and there is no pus or eyelash at its centre.
It is a blocked meibomian gland; warm compresses and lid massage are advised, with incision if it persists.
A 50-year-old woman visits her doctor about pain in her foot when walking.
She says it feels like there is a small stone in her shoe.
She wears narrow high-heeled shoes for work every day.
There is a small, hard, yellowish area of thick skin on the top of her fifth toe.
Paring the area shows a hard central core, and normal skin lines continue across it, with no black dots.
It is caused by pressure and friction; it is pared down, and she is advised to wear wider shoes and use padding.
A 3-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she will not use her left arm.
She was fine an hour ago and did not fall.
Her father says he swung her up by her hands while crossing the street, and she cried straight away.
She holds the arm still at her side with the elbow slightly bent and the palm facing down.
There is no swelling or bruising, but she cries when anyone tries to turn her palm up.
The doctor turns her forearm and bends the elbow with a click, and minutes later she is reaching for toys.
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with fever and a sore throat for one day.
He vomited once and complains of a headache and tummy ache.
Two children in his class had a sore throat last week.
His tonsils are red and swollen with white patches, and his tongue is red with large bumps.
A red rash on his neck and chest feels like sandpaper, his cheeks are flushed, and the skin around his mouth is pale.
A rapid strep test is positive for group A Streptococcus, and he starts a 10-day course of penicillin.
A 19-year-old student is seen after she passed out at a blood donation centre.
She had been standing in a hot, crowded queue for a long time and skipped breakfast.
She has fainted once before, at the sight of blood during a school first-aid class.
Before falling, she felt hot, sweaty, sick, and her vision went grey.
She was out for less than a minute, woke up fully alert with no confusion, and did not bite her tongue.
Her ECG and examination are normal; she is taught to lie down and cross her legs at early warning signs.
A 25-year-old woman comes to the emergency department frightened by chest pain.
The pain has been there for three days and is sharp, on the left side of her chest.
She recently started a new gym routine with lots of push-ups.
The pain gets worse when she takes a deep breath, twists, or presses on the area.
Pressing on the joints where her second to fourth ribs meet the breastbone reproduces the exact pain, without any swelling.
Her ECG and chest X-ray are normal; it is inflammation of the rib cartilage, and she is given anti-inflammatories and rest.
A 68-year-old man visits his doctor about burning pain on the right side of his chest.
The pain started four days ago and feels like a burn, even under light clothing.
He had chickenpox as a child and has been under a lot of stress lately.
Two days after the pain began, a red rash appeared in the same area.
The rash is a band of grouped blisters wrapping from his spine to the front of his chest, stopping at the midline.
He starts valaciclovir within 72 hours of the rash, and pain relief is arranged; the vaccine is advised once he recovers.
A 55-year-old man comes to the clinic with a painful leg.
He has had a fever and chills since yesterday.
He has diabetes and cracked skin between his toes from athlete's foot.
His lower leg is red, hot, swollen, and tender.
The red area has a poorly defined edge, and it has spread beyond the pen line drawn this morning.
Ultrasound excludes a clot, and he starts antibiotics against streptococci and staphylococci, such as flucloxacillin.
A 35-year-old teacher calls in sick in the middle of winter.
He says he felt fine yesterday morning but was suddenly hit by illness in the afternoon.
Many students in his school have been off with something similar this week.
He has a high fever, chills, severe muscle aches, and a pounding headache.
A dry cough and sore throat follow, and he feels too exhausted to get out of bed.
A nasal swab PCR is positive for an orthomyxovirus type A; he rests, drinks fluids, and is told to get the yearly vaccine.
A 23-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by friends because he is acting strangely.
They say he became confused, irritable, and slurred his words during a football match.
He has type 1 diabetes, took his usual insulin dose, and skipped lunch.
He is pale, shaking, sweating heavily, and his heart is racing.
A finger-prick glucose reading is 2.4 mmol/L (43 mg/dL).
He recovers within minutes after an IV glucose push and is advised to eat and check his sugar before exercise.
A 16-year-old rugby player is taken off the field during a match.
He collided head-to-head with another player and seemed dazed for a moment.
He did not lose consciousness, but he cannot remember the play just before the collision.
He complains of a headache, feeling dizzy, and being sensitive to light and noise.
His neurological exam is normal, and he has no repeated vomiting or worsening symptoms.
No scan is needed; he rests and returns to sport step by step once he is free of symptoms.
A 20-year-old student comes in because she has been feeling miserable for a few weeks.
She says it happens every spring and makes it hard to focus on her studies.
She had eczema as a child, and her brother has asthma.
She has a runny, blocked nose, sneezing fits, and itchy, watery eyes.
Her nasal lining is pale and swollen, and she has dark circles under her eyes.
Skin-prick testing is positive for grass pollen; she starts a steroid nasal spray and a non-sedating antihistamine.
A 66-year-old woman visits her doctor about knee pain that has bothered her for several years.
The pain gets worse with walking and climbing stairs and eases with rest.
She is overweight and used to work as a cleaner, kneeling for many hours.
Her knees are stiff for about 15 minutes in the morning and creak when she moves them.
Her knees are bony and enlarged, without warmth, and X-rays show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis.
She starts weight loss, physiotherapy, and topical anti-inflammatories, with knee replacement as a later option.
A 55-year-old woman visits the eye clinic about uncomfortable eyes.
She says her eyes feel gritty and burning, especially by the end of the day.
She works long hours on a computer in an air-conditioned office and recently went through menopause.
Her vision blurs at times but clears when she blinks.
The eyes look mildly red, and the tear film breaks up quickly on slit-lamp examination with fluorescein.
A Schirmer test shows low tear production; she starts artificial tears and screen breaks.
A 16-year-old girl is brought in by her mother because she misses school once a month.
She gets cramping lower tummy pain that spreads to her back and thighs.
The pain started about a year after her periods began.
It starts a few hours before her period and lasts for the first two days, with nausea and loose stools.
Her pelvic exam and ultrasound are normal.
Her pain improves with an NSAID started a day before her period, and a hormonal pill is offered if needed.
A 34-year-old warehouse worker visits his doctor about pain that started yesterday.
He felt a sudden twinge while lifting a heavy box with a twisted back.
The pain is in his lower back and gets worse when he bends, sits for long, or turns.
The muscles beside his spine are tight and tender, and moving hurts.
He has no leg weakness, numbness, bladder or bowel problems, fever, or weight loss.
No scan is needed; he is told to stay active, use simple painkillers and heat, and expect recovery within weeks.
A 24-year-old man visits his doctor feeling tired and sick for a week.
He has a low fever, has lost his appetite, and feels pain under his right ribs.
He came back three weeks ago from a backpacking trip where he ate street food and drank tap water.
